articles.title: New report identifies Hong Kong’s place in world shipping
articles.summary: Hong Kong Maritime Week is about to kick off. To celebrate the occasion, Splash today publishes a 48-page magazine on the city’s maritime hub credentials. A ship can be ordered at a mainland Chinese yard, owned through a leasing company in Hong Kong, insured in London, crewed through a management operation in Asia...
articles.body: Contributions Greater China New report identifies Hong Kong’s place in world shipping Splash November 13, 2026 0 559 8 minutes read Hong Kong Maritime Week is about to kick off. To celebrate the occasion, Splash today publishes a 48-page magazine on the city’s maritime hub credentials. A ship can be ordered at a mainland Chinese yard, owned through a leasing company in Hong Kong, insured in London, crewed through a management operation in Asia and chartered from Singapore. Its cargo need never pass through Hong Kong’s harbour. Even its Hong Kong financing vehicle may have to seek credit approval elsewhere. The geography of shipping has always been complicated. What has changed is the urgency with which Hong Kong must ask where the real business takes place. Is the city still a maritime capital in its own right, chosen by international owners, traders and financiers because of what it offers? Or is it becoming a highly sophisticated services counter for the vast industrial and commercial machine next door? On paper, the answer looks reassuring. Hong Kong remains fourth in the 2026 Xinhua-Baltic international maritime centre rankings, behind Singapore, Shanghai and London. Three of the world’s leading shipmanagement companies are headquartered here, major P&I clubs operate here, and the city retains a formidable concentration of lawyers, financiers and technical expertise. Look towards the waterfront, however, and a different picture emerges. The container port handled 12.99m teu in 2025, scarcely half its 2008 peak. The register has shed substantial tonnage amid geopolitical upheaval, falling to 109m gt by June this year. Shanghai, Shenzhen and Guangzhou have grown into maritime giants whose physical advantages Hong Kong cannot realistically overturn. These are not contradictory stories. Together they define the central question running through this special report: whether Hong Kong can convert its inherited maritime strengths into a sustainable business model for 2030, even as its traditional measures of importance become less flattering. Richard Hext, chairman of the Hong Kong Shipowners Association, resists the suggestion that the city is being reduced to an adjunct of the mainland. “An ‘annex’ does not host three of the world’s top 10 shipmanagers, 11 of the 12 International Group P&I associations, eight of the top ten ship-finance bookrunners,” he says, pointing also to the city’s legal institutions and international industry organisations. This inventory represents decades of investment and commercial trust. Yet it does not settle the more difficult question of what those institutions actually do here, or whether their next expansion will take place somewhere else. Where the decisions are made Hong Kong has spent much of this decade making itself more attractive on tax. Qualifying ship lessors can enjoy a zero profits-tax rate; eligible ship leasing managers, shipmanagers, agents and brokers benefit from half-rate treatment, as do certain marine insurers. The administration has also sought to broaden the proposition to physical commodity traders, recognising that traders create demand for chartering, insurance, finance and legal services The first results are tangible, but open to interpretation. Government figures show the number of ship leasing enterprises under the relevant preferential regime rising from 11 in 2020/21 to 46 in 2022/23. That is evidence that structures and businesses have responded. It says much less about the location of credit committees, the people selecting vessels or the teams negotiating charters. “Tax is necessary but not sufficient,” Hext says. Companies, he argues, follow customers, skills, capital and regulatory certainty. He wants the next phase judged by “regional headquarters, underwriting authority, credit decisions, trading desks and skilled jobs, and not by company registrations alone”. Gautam Chellaram, chairman of KC Maritime, is more sceptical about what tax reform has delivered. He sees genuine growth in leasing and mainland-linked finance, but says: “I do not yet see clear evidence that the measures have resulted in substantial headquarters relocation involving decision-makers, fund managers, and independent shipowners physically basing themselves in Hong Kong.” It would be equally wrong to dismiss the developments as bookkeeping. Hong Kong is a place where ships are managed, risks assessed and capital arranged, not merely where documents are signed. Dockendale Group is among the companies expanding management operations locally. Its chief executive, Vikrant Gusain, says Hong Kong’s ease of doing business is an important factor in the decision, alongside access to Asian markets and international talent. The competitive comparison nevertheless remains Singapore. “Singapore continues to offer broader tax incentives and a larger concentration of commodity traders,” says Jim James, senior consultant at Hill Dickinson. The latter point may be more important than the former. Traders and charterers bring transactions, and transactions bring the brokers, lenders, insurers and lawyers who serve them. A critical mass of principals is extraordinarily difficult to manufacture through concessions alone. Hong Kong has distinct advantages of its own. Its banking network connects Chinese and international capital; its offshore renminbi role creates opportunities for trade and leasing; and its links with a vast manufacturing and shipbuilding hinterland provide access that a competing maritime centre cannot reproduce. But geographical proximity is not the same thing as commercial gravity. The city must persuade companies to put people with mandates and budgets here, not just a local subsidiary. June’s tax amendment bill, including a proposed half-rate concession for qualifying physical commodity trading, gives the policy another push. September’s first five-year plan adds a ‘Finance + Maritime’ agenda built around ship finance, insurance, trade finance and related services. Neither initiative can be called successful solely because it exists. Their test will be new trading desks, lending decisions and customers with genuine freedom to transact elsewhere. The mainland advantage — and the danger Where does this leave the argument that Hong Kong is becoming Shanghai’s professional-services annex? Chellaram offers the report’s most uncomfortable formulation: as a cargo port, the city is being functionally subordinated to mainland competitors, but as a financial, legal and arbitration centre it retains qualities not available in the same combination across the border. “On the professional-services side, Hong Kong is the piece Shanghai structurally cannot replicate,” he says. The separate customs territory, common-law system, freely convertible currency and established international business practices all give the city a distinctive purpose. The opportunity is to sell those qualities to the world, not simply to companies moving through China. Damien Laracy, partner and head of Hill Dickinson’s Hong Kong office, describes a transition “from a cargo-driven port hub to a specialised centre for maritime services”. Rather than an annex, he sees “the region’s high-value maritime services platform, complementing the manufacturing, cargo, and port capacity of neighbouring cities”. The distinction is subtle but critical. A law firm advising a mainland shipowner on a vessel financing can be doing genuine international business from Hong Kong. So can an insurer handling a casualty thousands of miles away or a manager overseeing a fleet trading between Brazil and India. But the city’s position becomes more vulnerable if its principal attraction is merely that it makes mainland transactions easier. The international test is whether owners and counterparties with no direct mainland connection still choose Hong Kong. The machinery of a genuine maritime centre is already here. English-language maritime contracts, established common-law precedents, internationally recognised arbitration and access to mainland enforcement arrangements give it a credible offering. Rosita Lau, a partner at Ince, is among those urging the city to promote its legal and dispute-resolution capabilities far more systematically. The fact that Hong Kong can be chosen in a contract is not proof that it will be. There are also more prosaic measures of legal competitiveness. Martyn Huckerby, head of competition law and regulatory at Hill Dickinson, points to the extension of the block exemption for liner vessel-sharing agreements to 2031. The renewal, he says, preserves “legal certainty for operational cooperation between liner shipping companies”. It is a narrow regulatory decision, but one of the many predictable rules on which internationally mobile businesses build long-term operations. Insurance offers another illustration of integration without inevitable subordination. London P&I has served shipowners from Hong Kong for decades and opened an office in Shanghai in 2025. Deborah Yu, its regional director for Asia, says the two offices work together with the club’s operations in London and Athens. The point is not to force every Asian insurance decision into Hong Kong, but to ensure the city continues to handle work that could plausibly be located elsewhere. International outlook An international city must keep choosing to be international. That means foreign owners can operate comfortably, specialist staff can build careers and global counterparties can trust their contracts, information and capital to an environment they understand. This issue explores what that requirement means in practice. Hong Kong’s shipmanagement concentration provides a genuine strategic asset: it would take years to reproduce the crewing, technical and training networks that leading managers have built here. The challenge is keeping enough experienced people to make decisions locally as digitalisation, alternative fuels and increasingly complex compliance change the skill set. The same logic applies to finance and insurance. An internationally recognised logo on a Hong Kong office does not tell us whether it can approve a ship loan or underwrite a specialist risk. A registry’s gross tonnage does not establish where the family that owns the ship runs its business. A port’s box count says little about the value of transactions governed by local law, but the loss of container activity cannot be waved away simply by relabelling the city a services centre. Technology adds a further test. Hong Kong’s Port Community System is meant to help connect cargo movements, documentation and financing across the supply chain. But common platforms are only as useful as the trust and security behind them. Paul Haswell, technology partner at Hill Dickinson, notes that digitisation will bring “increased emphasis on data security and the monitoring of systems”. A financial and logistics crossroads cannot afford to treat cyber resilience as an optional extra. The city’s new maritime ambitions, particularly green bunkering and transition finance, depend on the same mixture of hard infrastructure and intangible trust. There is little value in promoting alternative fuels unless ships can take them safely, on schedule and at competitive prices. There is little point marketing green ship finance unless lenders and owners are prepared to commit capital against realistic assumptions about technology, fuel availability and earnings. Government has clearly recognised the need to change. Its first five-year plan shifts the emphasis from volume to value, promising stronger maritime services, a greener and smarter port, closer links with the Greater Bay Area and a more developed marine finance ecosystem. The question is no longer whether officials have ambitions. It is whether businesses can see projects proceeding quickly enough, and with sufficient commercial substance, to justify staying and expanding. That demands a sharper understanding of competition. Singapore can be a partner and a rival. Shanghai can be a customer, collaborator and competitor. The Greater Bay Area can supply Hong Kong with enormous commercial opportunities while simultaneously taking cargo, talent and investment from it. Those apparently inconsistent propositions are the reality of a maritime industry in which business moves wherever the overall proposition is strongest. The defensible future is neither a nostalgic campaign to win back every container nor a comfortable acceptance of being the mainland’s legal and financial back office. It is a city that remains indispensable to international shipping because substantive work is done there: ships are managed, cargo is traded, capital is committed, risks are insured and disputes are resolved. By 2030, Hong Kong should be judged less by how many companies have an address in Central or how many development plans have been published, and more by who has authority to do business from the city. Are the next fleet acquisitions decided here? Are traders locating profitable operations here? Are international parties choosing Hong Kong law when they have no obligation to do so? Are young maritime professionals staying because the best opportunities are available here? A gateway is somewhere business passes through. A maritime capital is somewhere business chooses to stay. Hong Kong has spent generations proving it can be both. The coming four years will show whether it still can. You can read the magazine ahead of Hong Kong Maritime Week by clicking here . articles.title: Maersk’s cyber breach is a warning for every secondhand ship sale
articles.summary: The door was a system that came with an acquisition. Every owner who buys a secondhand vessel takes the same risk on board, and few check for it at delivery. By Argyris Zafeiropoulos from Athens-based Resilience & Compliance Advisory. On November 11 Maersk confirmed that attackers had entered a local legacy system...
articles.body: Contributions Tech Maersk’s cyber breach is a warning for every secondhand ship sale Splash November 13, 2026 0 18 3 minutes read Maersk Line Maersk Line The door was a system that came with an acquisition. Every owner who buys a secondhand vessel takes the same risk on board, and few check for it at delivery. By Argyris Zafeiropoulos from Athens-based Resilience & Compliance Advisory. On November 11 Maersk confirmed that attackers had entered a local legacy system “inherited through a previous acquisition” and taken data from it. The company says the breach was confined to that system and that customer and partner connections were not affected. It has not named the business. A ransomware group calling itself WhiteArmor claims to hold about 100 GB from a platform linked to LF Logistics, which Maersk bought for $3.6bn in 2022, and wants $5m. None of that is verified. The facts will settle in time. The lesson is already clear, and it is not about Maersk. A system that arrives with an acquisition brings its own passwords, its own remote connections and its own suppliers, while the people who knew them leave with the seller. If the claim is right, that door had been open for four years. Shipping does the same thing every week, with ships. A second-hand bulker changes hands with its class certificates, its trading record and the documents listed in the memorandum of agreement. It also arrives with things no saleform lists: the administrator accounts on the bridge and engine-room computers, the engine maker’s remote-service link, the satellite terminal and its user accounts, the planned-maintenance software and whoever still holds a login to it, the crew network set up by the previous manager’s IT contractor. The buyer’s superintendent checks the hull, the machinery and the paperwork. Few delivery protocols carry a line that says all passwords changed, all of the seller’s remote access removed, all standing vendor connections listed. The same happens without a sale. A change of technical manager moves the ship onto new systems and new people, while the old manager’s accounts often stay on board until someone notices them. None of this is exotic, and the rules already reach it. Since 2021 cyber risk has had to be addressed in each company’s safety management system under the ISM Code. Ships contracted from July 2024 must meet the IACS unified requirements E26 and E27 on cyber resilience, but the second-hand tonnage changing hands today was mostly built before that. In the EU, NIS2 brings shipping companies above a size threshold within its scope, with an early warning due within 24 hours of a significant incident and a fuller notification within 72. That is where inheritance becomes expensive. An owner who finds an intrusion through a system nobody knew was there has to explain, against those deadlines, what the system was, who had access and why it was still connected. “It came with the ship” is an explanation. It is not evidence of control. The fix costs little and fits into work owners already do. Three steps cover most of it. First, put it in the inspection. A cyber section in the pre-purchase inspection that lists the networked systems on board, their makers and who has remote access to them takes a few hours, and gives the buyer leverage while the price is still open. Second, put it in the delivery protocol. At handover every administrator password is changed, every remote account of the seller and its contractors is closed, and every connection that stays, the engine maker’s or the ECDIS supplier’s, is confirmed in writing with the buyer named as the new owner. Third, write it down with a date. A short record signed at delivery of what was found, what was changed and what was kept. If something goes wrong a year later, that record is the difference between showing the door was locked and hoping it was. Maersk will get through this; it got through NotPetya in 2017, which cost it up to $300m. An owner with ten ships, half of them bought second-hand, has less room. The cheapest moment to find out what came with a ship is the day it changes hands. articles.title: Kalmar secures order for 21 hybrid straddle carriers at TTI Algeciras
articles.summary: Kalmar has secured an order from Total Terminal International Algeciras (TTI Algeciras) for 21 hybrid straddle carriers. The new equipment will support shuttle carrier operations at the Spanish container terminal. The order was recorded in Kalmar’s fourth-quarter 2026 order intake, with deliveries expected to be...
articles.body: Kalmar has secured an order from Total Terminal International Algeciras (TTI Algeciras) for 21 hybrid straddle carriers. The new equipment will support shuttle carrier operations at the Spanish container terminal. The order was recorded in Kalmar’s fourth-quarter 2026 order intake, with deliveries expected to be completed during the fourth quarter of 2027. The company did not disclose the value of the agreement. TTI Algeciras operates one of the two container terminals at the Port of Algeciras Bay. It was also the first semi-automated container terminal in Southern Europe. The terminal is currently undergoing an expansion project that aims to increase its handling capacity to 2.1 million TEUs by 2028. Located near the Strait of Gibraltar, the facility can accommodate both existing and next-generation ultra-large container vessels (ULCVs). Its equipment fleet currently includes 23 Kalmar straddle carriers. Kalmar expands its presence at TTI Algeciras The latest order strengthens an existing relationship between Kalmar and TTI Algeciras. In addition to supplying cargo-handling equipment, Kalmar provides maintenance services at the terminal. The companies recently signed a separate Kalmar Care agreement covering mechanical maintenance for eight ship-to-shore (STS) cranes and 32 automated stacking cranes (ASCs). The agreement includes both preventive and corrective maintenance. “Our long-term partnership with Kalmar has consistently delivered the performance we expect. Choosing their hybrid straddle carriers once again was a strategic decision to further enhance our terminal’s efficiency and continue our commitment to sustainable operations at TTI Algeciras,” said Alonso Luque Jimenez, CEO, TTI Algeciras. The additional hybrid straddle carriers will support the terminal’s efforts to improve efficiency and reduce the environmental impact of its operations. “We are very proud to continue our successful collaboration with TTI Algeciras. This order for 21 of our hybrid straddle carriers for shuttle carrier operations is a testament to the operational reliability and productivity our solutions bring to their terminal, further supporting their ambition to set the standard for efficient, sustainable operations in the region,” said Sergio Peralta, Country Director, Spain, Kalmar. The equipment order comes as TTI Algeciras continues its terminal expansion programme, which is expected to increase its container-handling capacity by 2028.

articles.title: MPA opens applications for LNG floating storage unit licences
articles.summary: The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore has opened applications for licences to operate up to two LNG Floating Storage Units in Singapore anchorages. The call follows MPA’s award of eight new LNG bunker supplier licences in July 2026. The FSUs are intended to complement the expanded supplier base by diversifying...
articles.body: The Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore has opened applications for licences to operate up to two LNG Floating Storage Units in Singapore anchorages. The call follows MPA’s award of eight new LNG bunker supplier licences in July 2026. The FSUs are intended to complement the expanded supplier base by diversifying LNG storage and reloading options, supporting the continued growth of LNG bunkering in Singapore and strengthening supply resilience. Applications are open to existing LNG bunker licensees, who may partner with third-party terminal operators to provide storage and operational expertise. Most of each FSU’s storage capacity must be allocated to LNG bunkering, and a minimum share must be made available to other LNG bunker suppliers on open-access terms. Applicants must own or charter at least one FSU with a minimum storage capacity of 130,000 cubic metres, registered with the Singapore Registry of Ships and compliant with MPA’s safety and operational requirements. Operators must also disclose to MPA the maximum fees they intend to charge for LNG reloading services. Each licence will be valid for five years. To support the decarbonisation of international shipping, the FSUs must also be certified under the International Sustainability and Carbon Certification European Union framework so that they can handle bio-LNG and e-LNG. This will allow the infrastructure to support the supply of these lower-emission LNG alternatives as they become more widely available.

articles.title: DSV and Google Cloud partner on sustainable aviation fuel
articles.summary: DSV has entered into a collaboration with Google Cloud to support the use of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) in air freight operations, with the agreement covering up to 9.7 million litres of fuel and targeting a reduction of 25,000 tonnes of lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions compared with conventional jet fuel. The...
articles.body: DSV has entered into a collaboration with Google Cloud to support the use of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) in air freight operations, with the agreement covering up to 9.7 million litres of fuel and targeting a reduction of 25,000 tonnes of lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions compared with conventional jet fuel. The initiative focuses on a key air freight route used for Google Cloud shipments and will initially operate as a pilot project, providing a potential foundation for broader cooperation between the two companies on transport emissions. According to DSV, the SAF used under the agreement is produced from waste and residue feedstocks and offers an 85% reduction in lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions compared with conventional fossil-based aviation fuel. The collaboration comes as the logistics and aviation sectors seek to expand access to lower-emission fuels, although limited SAF availability remains a challenge to wider adoption. “Our customers want practical ways to lower the emissions of the goods they move. By combining Google Cloud’s ambition with our SAF programme, we turn a sustainability goal into measurable results in air freight,” said Frank Sobotka, CEO, Air & Sea Division, DSV. Book-and-claim approach supports emissions accounting The agreement uses a book-and-claim methodology, allowing Google Cloud to receive the environmental attributes associated with SAF consumption without requiring the fuel to be physically used on the aircraft transporting its shipments. Under this approach, emissions reductions can be allocated to a specific customer independently of the location where the sustainable fuel is consumed. “This collaboration builds on our ongoing efforts to reduce emissions across Google Cloud’s global logistics operations. Partnering on sustainable aviation fuel provides an auditable, transparent mechanism to address air freight emissions while helping accelerate commercial demand for lower-carbon fuels,” said Brian Stewart, Senior Director, Logistics, Google Cloud. The SAF is certified under the International Sustainability and Carbon Certification (ISCC) scheme and is produced exclusively from waste and residue materials, excluding palm oil and palm-derived feedstocks. Environmental attributes associated with the fuel are issued, transferred and retired through the independent Sustainable Aviation Fuel Certificate Registry (SAFc Registry), alongside DSV’s internal tracking systems. According to the company, the certification and tracking arrangements are designed to ensure that each tonne of CO₂e reduction is allocated to an individual shipper and is not counted more than once. The pilot also represents an effort to support commercial demand for SAF, with commitments from logistics providers and their customers potentially contributing to the expansion of sustainable fuel production and availability.

articles.title: US ethanol readily available to fuel the world’s methanol-capable fleet
articles.summary: Ethanol can use the dual-fuel engines and bunkering infrastructure built for methanol with limited modification. That gives shipowners a readily available fuel for a growing fleet at a time when supply of low-emission methanol remains constrained, according to a new study published today by the Maritime Ethanol &...
articles.body: US ethanol readily available to fuel the world’s methanol-capable fleet in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 13/11/2026 Ethanol can use the dual-fuel engines and bunkering infrastructure built for methanol with limited modification. That gives shipowners a readily available fuel for a growing fleet at a time when supply of low-emission methanol remains constrained, according to a new study published today by the Maritime Ethanol & Methanol Alliance (MEMA), a platform of the Global Centre for Green Fuels (GCGF). According to the study, Marine Ethanol: Unlocking the US Opportunity, ethanol can support the more than 300 methanol-capable vessels in service or on order, either on its own or blended with methanol. The study adds that the US is well placed to meet shipping’s growing demand for biofuels. US plants can produce 18.5 billion gallons a year against 2025 output of 16.4 billion gallons, leaving around 2 billion gallons of spare capacity. The US already produces just over half of the world’s fuel ethanol. It exports to around 80 countries, largely through Gulf Coast terminals that are also major bunkering hubs. International shipping burns around 300 million tonnes of fuel a year, worth an estimated US$180 billion. In the study’s illustrative scenarios, ethanol meeting 1% of that fuel by mass would require around 1 billion gallons, well within today’s spare capacity. A 5% share by the mid-2030s would require around 5 billion gallons. The study comes as ethanol bunkering moves from trials to commercial operation. On 28 September, Tangier Maersk completed a commercial ship-to-ship bunkering of US corn ethanol in Houston, the first publicly announced US ethanol bunkering of a deep-sea container vessel. The International Maritime Organization, shipping’s global regulator, is expected to decide next steps on its Net-Zero Framework at an extraordinary session on 4 December, directly after MEPC 85. The study assesses ethanol at technology readiness level 8–9: technically mature, with commercial deployment emerging. Compared with heavy fuel oil, ethanol virtually eliminates sulphur oxide emissions. It cuts nitrogen oxides by 40–94%, depending on engine technology, and particulate matter by 90–99%, without scrubbers. Its net production cost, after co-product revenue, is below US$1 a gallon, which is low relative to other low-emission marine fuels. The study is published by MEMA, a platform of the Global Centre for Green Fuels. ABS provided the technical analysis as Knowledge Partner. The views and recommendations in the study are those of MEMA. US ethanol producer Marquis Energy provided industry input. Clarence Woo, Managing Director of the Global Centre for Green Fuels, said: “Ethanol is moving beyond pilots, and this study shows the United States has the production base and export infrastructure to supply shipping at scale. The next challenge is consistency. As international bunkering grows, shipping needs standardised and fungible marine fuel specifications, together with traceable feedstocks and a robust chain of custody, so that ethanol from different producers and regions can be used with confidence.” The full report can be downloaded from www.green-fuels.org/us-ethanol Source: Global Centre for Green Fuels (GCGF) 2026-11-13 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Newbuilding Contracting Activity Remains Elevated in Hellenic Shipping News 13/11/2026 M ore newbuilding orders have continued to pour into global shipyards, as owners are looking to increase their exposure to both the wet and the dry bulk markets. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Intermodal said that “on the dry side, A.E. Nomikos placed an order for an 82k dwt bulker at Oshima Shipbuilding for delivery in 2030. On the tanker front, CSET commissioned 6 LNG ready, 309k dwt, VLCCs at COSCO HI Yangzhou and 4 more at DSIC, scheduled for delivery across 2029-2030. Stealth Maritime also ordered 2 VLCCs of 320k dwt at Hanwha Ocean for 2030 delivery at $133m each and 2 LR2s of 115k dwt at HD Hyundai HI, due in 2029-2030, at $78m per vessel. Laskaridis Tankers added 2 LR2s of 114k dwt at Hengli Shipbuilding due in 2028. Leon Shipping & Trading contracted 2 tankers of 50k dwt at COSCO Guangdong for $52.9m each, due in 2029, while Orkim Shipping secured 2 tankers of 9k dwt at Fujian Southeast with delivery between 2028-2029 for $18.8m each”. Source: Intermodal shipbroker Meanwhile, “in containerships, TS Lines booked 2 units of 11k teu at SWS, for 2030 delivery, valued at $123m each. In addition, Eastern Pacific ordered 2 boxships of 9k teu and 2 more units of 6k teu at Imabari Shipbuilding, both due in 2030, at $100m and $80m per unit, respectively. Peter Döhle Group added 4 containerships of 3.7k teu at Chengxi Shipyard due in 2029, built to NOx Tier III, EEDI Phase III and SOx-compliant standards. Samudera Shipping placed an order for 2 units of 3k teu at Yangzijiang Shipbuilding with delivery in 2030, while PIL inked 7 methanol ready feeders of 1.4k teu at Huanghai Shipbuilding with delivery spanning 2029-2030. In gas carriers, Foresight Group booked 4 LPG/Ammonia carriers of 90k cbm capacity at HD Hyundai HI with a delivery window of 2029-2030 for $117.5m each. Benelux Overseas also signed for 2 units of 48k cbm at CSSC Guangzhou Huangpu Wenchong due in 2030”, Intermodal concluded. articles.title: LR2s Turn Dirty: A larger fleet, but fewer LR2s trading clean
articles.summary: Dirty Employment Gains Ground The LR2 market has undergone a marked change in vessel employment since the start of 2025. Signal Ocean data show that dirty employment accounted for 74.2% of the LR2 fleet on 30 October 2026, compared with 53.0% on 1 January 2025. The shift accelerated in 2026, reducing the number of...
articles.body: LR2s Turn Dirty: A larger fleet, but fewer LR2s trading clean in International Shipping News 13/11/2026 D irty Employment Gains Ground The LR2 market has undergone a marked change in vessel employment since the start of 2025. Signal Ocean data show that dirty employment accounted for 74.2% of the LR2 fleet on 30 October 2026, compared with 53.0% on 1 January 2025. The shift accelerated in 2026, reducing the number of LR2s in clean trades even as the overall fleet expanded. Dirty-employed LR2s rose from 256 to 402 vessels, an increase of 57%, while clean-employed tonnage fell from 227 to 140, a reduction of 38%. Over the same period, the combined LR2 count grew from 483 to 542 vessels. A larger fleet has therefore delivered fewer clean ships. LR2 employment at a glance Daily vessel counts by employment. 30 October 2026 is the latest change in the series; counts are unchanged to 7 November 2026. Chart 1. LR2 vessels in dirty and clean employment, and the dirty share of the LR2 fleet, 1 January 2025–30 October 2026. Source: Signal Ocean Platform, LR2 employment data. During the first half of 2025, LR2 employment remained relatively balanced between clean and dirty trades. Clean-employed vessels outnumbered dirty units between 20 July and 17 October 2025, with the dirty share falling to 47.1% on 22 August. However, the subsequent increase in dirty employment marked a notable change in fleet deployment, with more LR2 capacity shifting away from clean petroleum product trades. The most significant adjustment occurred between January and April 2026, when dirty-employed LR2s increased by 82 vessels, compared with a reduction of 60 vessels in clean employment. This raised the dirty share from 55.3% to 68.9% in just four months. Since 23 July, the share has remained above 70%, suggesting a more persistent redistribution of LR2 capacity towards dirty trades rather than a short-lived change in employment patterns. Deployment: Relet and Spot Drive the Dirty Build The breakdown by employment type provides further insight into the redistribution of LR2 capacity. Within dirty trades, relet employment recorded the largest increase, rising from 43 to 125 vessels, followed by gains in spot (+46) and programme employment (+32). In contrast, the clean segment experienced its largest reduction in spot employment, where vessel numbers declined from 113 to 64. Chart 2. Change in LR2 count by market deployment and employment, 1 January 2025 to 30 October 2026. Source: Signal Ocean Platform, LR2 employment data by market deployment. In our interpretation, the near-tripling of dirty relet tonnage points to a meaningful part of the shift taking place through relet arrangements rather than purely through spot fixing. The employment data record deployment type only; they do not show the underlying contractual or pooling arrangements. For clean product markets, the contraction of the spot list matters most, as prompt spot tonnage is most directly exposed to daily freight. LR2 Employment Shifts Accelerate in 2026 Weekly LR2 employment figures show a sustained reduction in clean-employed tonnage since October 2025, with the decline accelerating during 2026. The clean-employed fleet fell by a net 6 vessels in 2025, compared with a much larger decline of 82 vessels in the first ten months of 2026. The largest weekly reduction occurred in the week ending 20 March 2026, when clean employment fell by 14 vessels, while dirty trades rose by 16 vessels. Chart 3. Week-on-week change in clean-employed LR2s, Friday to Friday, weeks ending 17 January 2025–30 October 2026 (94 weekly changes; base Friday 10 January 2025). Annual net changes use calendar endpoints. Source: Signal Ocean Platform, LR2 employment data; calculations by Signal Ocean Market Insights. The reduction continued into October, with five consecutive weekly declines ranging from 3 to 6 vessels. Although clean employment recorded occasional weekly increases, these were insufficient to offset the loss of tonnage. The contraction in clean-employed LR2 capacity, alongside growing dirty employment, has reduced the fleet available for clean petroleum product trades, with potential implications for vessel supply and freight conditions. Weekly changes in employment counts do not necessarily reflect direct shifts between clean and dirty trades, as fleet additions, removals and classification changes may also influence the figures. The Aframax Connection The combined Aframax/LR2 population offers a wider view of the supply balance. Dirty-employed vessels in this dataset population rose from 676 on 1 January 2026 to 800 on 30 October 2026, while clean-employed vessels declined from 233 to 149. The population’s dirty share reached 84.3%. Chart 4. Dirty share of the LR2 fleet and of the combined Aframax/LR2 dataset population, and population composition, 1 January 2025 and 30 October 2026. Source: Signal Ocean Platform, LR2 and Aframax/LR2 employment data. “Population” refers to the vessels covered by the Aframax/LR2 dataset, not a commercial pooling arrangement. “Other” = vessels in that population not counted as LR2s. The LR2 fleet is converging on the dirty profile of the wider Aframax/LR2 population: the gap between the two shares has narrowed from 23.2 to 10.1 percentage points. LR2s now account for 57% of the population, compared with 47% at the start of 2025, while vessels outside the LR2 count fell from 542 to 407. Only 9 clean ships remain outside the LR2 count, so clean Aframax-size availability is now almost entirely an LR2 question. Freight Implications: Fleet Growth Does Not Equal Available Supply For clean product markets, a smaller actively employed LR2 fleet may increase sensitivity to cargo demand, vessel positioning and regional imbalances. Even as the overall fleet grows, fewer vessels in clean trades can limit the market’s capacity to absorb additional product cargoes, particularly on long-haul routes. For dirty markets, increasing LR2 participation expands the supply of tonnage competing for crude and dirty petroleum product cargoes. The freight effect will depend on geographical deployment, cargo sizes, voyage duration and owners’ willingness to move vessels between markets. The cost and operational requirements of returning a dirty-employed vessel to clean service also matter. Tank cleaning, cargo suitability and commercial considerations mean that capacity to return to clean trades is not immediately available, so any tightness in clean tonnage could persist for some time once established. Market Takeaways The most significant development is not simply that more LR2s are trading dirty, but that the relationship between nominal fleet growth and effective clean tanker supply has changed. With more than 70% of the LR2 fleet in dirty trades, future shifts in LR2 employment could matter for both product tanker availability and Aframax-class dirty competition. Whether this pattern persists will depend on relative earnings, cargo demand and the commercial incentives for vessels to return to clean service. A sustained run of weekly gains in clean-employed LR2s would signal a potential reversal of the trend. For freight analysis, tracking LR2 employment between clean and dirty trades is becoming as important as monitoring the size of the fleet itself. Source: By Maria Bertzeletou, Signal Group, https://www.thesignalgroup.com/newsroom/market-insights-lr2s-turn-dirty-a-changing-balance-in-tanker-employment Tops 2026-11-13 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

The shift accelerated in 2026, reducing the number of LR2s in clean trades even as the overall fleet expanded.
Dirty-employed LR2s rose from 256 to 402 vessels, an increase of 57%, while clean-employed tonnage fell from 227 to 140, a reduction of 38%.

articles.title: Dry bulk ship recycling falls 36% to 18-year low
articles.summary: “Between January and October 2026, dry bulk ship recycling fell 36% y/y to 3m DWT, its lowest level in 18 years. Only 70 ships were recycled, primarily smaller ships in the handysize and supramax segments, as strong freight rates have extended the operational lives of older ships,” says Filipe Gouveia, Shipping...
articles.body: Dry bulk ship recycling falls 36% to 18-year low in International Shipping News 13/11/2026 “B etween January and October 2026, dry bulk ship recycling fell 36% y/y to 3m DWT, its lowest level in 18 years. Only 70 ships were recycled, primarily smaller ships in the handysize and supramax segments, as strong freight rates have extended the operational lives of older ships,” says Filipe Gouveia, Shipping Analysis Manager at BIMCO. Dry bulk ship recycling has been at a low level since 2021 due to strong freight rates. Several disruptions have tightened the supply/demand balance. These include high congestion in 2021, longer sailing distances due to sanctions on Russian coal, which caused ships to be rerouted away from the Red Sea, and growing shipments from the Atlantic to Asia. More recently, strong investment in AI has supported electricity demand, coal consumption and global economic growth, helping the market withstand headwinds from changes in US trade policy and disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. “Following several years of low ship recycling levels, a significant overhang has built up. We estimate that if ship lifecycles had remained in line with those observed between 2000 and 2019, an additional 856 ships, totalling 61m DWT, would have been recycled by now. That is equivalent to 6% of the current fleet capacity. As ships remain in service for longer, the dry bulk fleet has gradually aged, with the average bulk carrier now over 13 years old, compared with an average of 10 years at the start of the decade,” says Gouveia. The recycling overhang is increasingly visible in the age profile of the fleet. There are now 1,035 dry bulk ships, totalling 46.7m DWT, which are more than 25 years old. These are equivalent to 7% of ships and 4% of fleet capacity. The share of older capacity is highest in the handysize and panamax segments, at 8% each, compared with 5% for supramax. By contrast, only 11 capesize ships are more than 25 years old, since capesizes typically have shorter lifecycles. In our latest Dry Bulk Shipping Market Overview & Outlook, we forecast the supply/demand balance to gradually weaken in 2027 and 2028, albeit from a high baseline. Ship deliveries are expected to accelerate, growing 19% in 2027 and a further 4% in 2028. The increase will be driven by the capesize segment, following higher contracting in recent years. “As market conditions gradually weaken, freight rates could soften, making it less attractive to keep older ships operating. Consequently, we estimate ship recycling could increase to 5.5m DWT in 2027 and 9.2m DWT in 2028, which would be the highest since 2020. Nevertheless, even with this increase, recycling levels would be low compared with the highs seen during the 2010s and an overhang of older ships would remain,” says Gouveia. articles.title: Remembering the role of our ports
articles.summary: Yesterday, on Remembrance Day, we remember all those who served, those who made the ultimate sacrifice, and the families and communities whose lives were changed by conflict. Throughout both World Wars, ports across ABP’s network played an important role in supporting Britain’s wartime efforts. During the First World...
articles.body: Remembering the role of our ports in Port News 13/11/2026 Yesterday, on Remembrance Day, we remember all those who served, those who made the ultimate sacrifice, and the families and communities whose lives were changed by conflict. Throughout both World Wars, ports across ABP’s network played an important role in supporting Britain’s wartime efforts. During the First World War, Southampton’s docks were requisitioned as Britain’s No. 1 Military Embarkation Port, becoming a major departure point for troops heading overseas. Immingham became a home base for Royal Navy submarines, while in Grimsby, fishing vessels and trawlers were requisitioned for naval service, with many taking on minesweeping and patrol duties. Cardiff’s docks also came under military control, with coal exports redirected to help supply the Royal Navy. Landing craft at the Port of Southampton These contributions continued during the Second World War. Southampton became a major embarkation point for the Allied invasion of Europe, with more than 3.5 million troops and over 250,000 vehicles embarking from the port between D-Day and the end of the war. Immingham once again served as a naval base, becoming the headquarters of the Royal Navy’s Flag Officer for the Humber. Grimsby became Britain’s largest minesweeping base, with vessels from the Royal Naval Patrol Service – known as ‘Churchill’s Pirates’ – working to clear mines and keep vital shipping routes open. Cardiff and Newport also played important roles in supporting the movement of military personnel and essential supplies. Loading tanks aboard the ‘Brisbane Star’ at the Port of Newport in 1942 Preserving our maritime history This history continues to be recognised today. In Southampton, ABP has helped preserve a historic ‘Whale’ bridge, originally designed as part of the Mulberry Harbour system developed to support the D-Day landings. These floating roadways were an important part of the temporary harbours used to transport troops, vehicles and supplies from ships to shore following the Allied invasion of Normandy. The surviving bridge was lifted from Southampton’s Town Quay in 2025 and relocated to Solent Gateway at Marchwood. Following specialist restoration, it was unveiled in October 2026, helping preserve an important piece of maritime and wartime engineering history. D-Day Mulberry Harbour ‘Whale’ memorial Conflict leaves a lasting legacy, and the history of our ports is a reminder of the people whose lives were shaped by it. articles.body: IMO may codify alternative net-zero bunker rules in 2027: US FMC in International Shipping News 13/11/2026 The International Maritime Organization (IMO) may start forming consensus around an alternative Net-Zero Framework (NZF) in the coming weeks before hammering out its final text in 2027, US Federal Maritime Commission Chairman Laura DiBella said. The UN agency is due to hold meetings Nov. 23-Dec. 4 to discuss the framework, after member states last year voted to delay its adoption by a year amid fierce US opposition. “I hope we’re going to come to some sort of landing spot,” DiBella told Platts on the sidelines of the International Bunker Industry Association’s annual convention in New York City. “I don’t think anything will be codified this year — maybe 2027, it will be codified. But I think we’ll come to some sort of consensus,” DiBella said. The comments from the top US maritime regulator came after Japan, Panama, and some other countries proposed several alternatives to the NZF, which, in its current form, would place a mandatory cost on maritime greenhouse gas emissions from 2028 to promote a low-carbon bunker transition. The US has estimated that the framework would cost the shipping industry $53 billion-$265 billion annually while arguing the incremental expenses would be ultimately passed on to businesses and consumers. “We have the potential to take remedial action against the flag states that support it, that deliver cargo to the US,” DiBella said, referring to the FMC’s remit. “As the largest consumer of imported goods, we will face the biggest penalties. We don’t need additional inflationary measures on our cargo.” But Washington would be open to what it believes to be a commercially realistic, technology-neutral NZF with achievable emissions targets, voluntary market-based compliance, and no mandatory carbon bills collected by the IMO, the US has suggested. “The United States is working toward a consensus on something so that industry can make the necessary investments [in alternative fuels] and move ahead,” DiBella said. Gas pathway DiBella has displayed a favorable attitude toward LNG and bio-LNG and previously said in a web post that based on her personal view, the fuels could meet over 60% of global maritime bunker demand by 2050, and that the US is well positioned to supply the fuels as the world’s top LNG exporter, which could draw investments in increasing bio-LNG output with a “well-designed global fuel standard. “The infrastructure is there to support it globally … I lean very heavy on the infrastructure side and what’s available and what’s realistic,” she told Platts, part of S&P Global Energy. October’s average bunker prices for 0.5%-sulfur fuel oil were $17.90/gigajoule in Rotterdam, compared with $28.78/GJ for LNG and $51.71/GJ for bio-LNG, according to the Platts global bunker cost calculator. articles.title: Korean partnership’s carbon capture proposal selected as basis for IMO’s future safety guidelines
articles.summary: A leading Korean public-private partnership comprising 10 maritime organizations has reached a major milestone in the development of international safety guidelines for onboard carbon capture and storage system (OCCS) after the proposal jointly developed by its members was selected as the base document for further...
articles.body: Korean partnership’s carbon capture proposal selected as basis for IMO’s future safety guidelines in International Shipping News 13/11/2026 A leading Korean public-private partnership comprising 10 maritime organizations has reached a major milestone in the development of international safety guidelines for onboard carbon capture and storage system (OCCS) after the proposal jointly developed by its members was selected as the base document for further development at the International Maritime Organization (IMO). At the IMO’s 12th session of the Sub-Committee on Carriage of Cargoes and Containers (CCC 12), the working group agreed to use the proposal from the Korean partnership as the basis for developing interim OCCS safety guidelines, incorporating elements of a separate proposal from the International Association of Classification Societies (IACS). Established in April 2026, the partnership is led by Korea’s Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries, with Korean Register (KR) overseeing regulatory development. Its members include HMM, Samsung Heavy Industries, Hanwha Ocean, HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering, Hyundai Heavy Industries Power Systems, HI Air Korea, PANASIA and the Korea Research Institute of Ships & Ocean Engineering (KRISO). Drawing on the partners’ operational, shipbuilding, manufacturing and research expertise, KR consolidated their technical contributions into a single regulatory proposal, which was submitted to the IMO through the Ministry. CCC 12 also agreed to establish the Correspondence Group on GHG Safety under Korea’s coordination to advance the guidelines. Joonghun Kim from KR’s Convention & Legislation Service Team has been named coordinator of the group and will bring together contributions from IMO Member States and international organizations to develop common safety requirements, with technology-specific annexes to be considered if time permits. The group will report its progress to CCC 13 in 2027. Kyung-bok Kim, Executive Vice President of KR, said: “The practical experience, knowledge and expertise of the entire 10-member partnership have led to an important milestone in the development of OCCS safety standards at an IMO level. Our next step is to bring contributions from Member States and international organizations together to develop workable safety requirements. “By leading the development of OCCS standards, Korea is leading the charge in the global decarbonization of the maritime industry, helping to ensure that safe, workable OCCS solutions become a practical reality for vessels worldwide,” he added. The proposal builds on Korea’s multi-year OCCS development work, including raising safety concerns about the location of onboard CO₂ storage tanks in 2023 and proposing initial safety guidelines in 2024. It also draws on technical assessments and operational experience associated with HMM Mongla, which was fitted with an OCCS solution in 2024 as part of a joint project involving HMM, Samsung Heavy Industries, PANASIA and KR. Ongoing risk assessments based on the vessel’s OCCS design identified 64 hazard scenarios, helping to inform the development of practical shipboard safety requirements. The proposed guidelines address how OCCS equipment can be safely integrated with a vessel’s structure, layout and machinery systems. They cover practical safety considerations including CO₂ handling and storage, leakage prevention, emergency response and the safe transfer of captured carbon ashore. These requirements are intended to address not only the capture equipment itself, but also its interaction with other onboard systems and day-to-day vessel operations. The framework retains a technology-neutral main body covering common safety requirements, alongside separate annexes addressing hazards specific to different OCCS technologies. This approach allows different capture methods, including chemical absorption, membrane separation and mineralization, to be considered without favoring a particular technology, while enabling requirements to evolve as further evidence becomes available. Speaking about the importance of reflecting real-world operational experience in the proposed guidelines, members of the Korean partnership highlighted the need for practical standards that reflect the realities of running OCCS systems at sea. Youngsun Kim, Senior Vice President, Director of Technology & Innovation Institute, HMM Co., Ltd., said: “Shipowners need standards covering safe operation, maintenance and offloading, not capture performance alone. It was important to be able to reflect actual operating conditions from an early stage of international guideline development.” Ho-ki Lee, Vice President at Samsung Heavy Industries, said: “At CCC 12, we saw growing consensus around onboard carbon capture as a practical option for decarbonizing shipping. Drawing on our experience in shipbuilding and OCCS demonstration, we will contribute to international safety guidelines that enable carbon capture systems to operate safely and efficiently on board ships.” Yoon-Sik Hwang, Vice President at Hanwha Ocean, said: “This joint proposal is particularly meaningful because it brings together expertise from shipbuilding, shipping, marine equipment and classification. Hanwha Ocean will continue contributing to the development of international safety guidelines, drawing on its demonstration experience and technical capabilities to accelerate the commercialization of onboard carbon capture technology.” Sangmin Park, Senior Vice President at HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering, said: “The acceptance of the Korean-led proposal on interim OCCS safety guidelines is a meaningful achievement towards the commercialization of onboard carbon capture technology. Drawing on the experience accumulated through OCCS technology development, HDKSOE will contribute to international safety guidelines to support the safe application of OCCS on ships.” Jeongsu Seo, Executive Director at HI AIR KOREA, said: “Safety functions must be capable of being tested and verified in the field. Drawing on our experience in developing and demonstrating mineralization-based capture technology, we will contribute to practical safety standards for both newbuildings and retrofits by linking that experience to leak detection and emergency shutdown requirements.” The Correspondence Group on GHG Safety will continue developing the draft guidelines ahead of CCC 13 in 2027, drawing on contributions from Member States and international organizations. The Korean partnership will support this work by contributing its members’ design, manufacturing and operating experience to the development of practical shipboard safety requirements. Finalization and approval of the interim guidelines will be subject to further consideration by the IMO. Source: Korean Register 2026-11-13 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: Established in April 2026, the partnership is led by Korea’s Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries, with Korean Register (KR) overseeing regulatory development.
CCC 12 also agreed to establish the Correspondence Group on GHG Safety under Korea’s coordination to advance the guidelines.
The group will report its progress to CCC 13 in 2027.

The platform focuses on shorter-duration employment, retaining flexibility to adjust chartering strategy to the changing market conditions. • Fleet renewal – sale of older tonnage : During Q3 2026, the Company completed the sale of the 2009-built Supramax Bermondi, recognizing a gain of approximately $2.5 million and releasing capital from older tonnage while preserving financial flexibility for future opportunities. • Debt refinancing: The Company has signed commitments for new loan facilities totaling $133 million, secured by 18 vessels in its existing fleet, which will refinance all of its existing loan obligations. The new arrangements are expected to reduce financing costs through lower margins and extend debt maturities from Q4 2029 (at the earliest) to between Q4 2031 and Q1 2032. Upon completion of the refinancings, the Company’s unencumbered fleet is expected to increase from 3 to 11 vessels. MANAGEMENT COMMENTARY Mr. Gregory Zikos, Chief Executive Officer of Costamare Bulkers Holdings Limited, commented: “During the third quarter of the year Costamare Bulkers generated net income of about $17 million. Following the transfer of the Company’s entire legacy trading portfolio to Cargill, we are now operating a Kamsarmax-focused trading platform, currently employing 32 vessels primarily chartered-in on short-term fixed rate charters, some of which include charterers’ extension options. As part of our fleet renewal program, we recently completed the sale of the 2009-built Supramax Bermondi, recognizing a capital gain of about $2.5 million. Regarding our balance sheet, we have signed commitments for new loan facilities totaling $133 million, essentially refinancing all our existing debt. The new arrangements are expected to reduce financing costs and extend our debt maturities from 2029 out to 2031-2032, while increasing our unencumbered fleet from 3 to 11 vessels. With total cash exceeding debt by approximately $142 million, the Company is net cash positive, positioning us favorably to grow countercyclically in a low asset value environment. The dry bulk market was characterized by heightened volatility during the quarter. In the Capesize segment, an active typhoon season tightened tonnage supply through vessel delays and congestion in China, and the upward market extended into September, supported by strong Guinean bauxite exports despite the rainy season. The Panamax market remained relatively strong throughout the quarter, although rates briefly corrected in the second half of July as typhoon-related congestion in China eased, the corresponding Capesize market correction reduced support for the Panamax market, and Black Sea disruption weighed on grain flows. Finally, the Supramax index continued its gradual upward trend, supported by vessel inefficiencies and the strong larger-segment market, notwithstanding a brief correction from late July to mid-August due to a corresponding Capesize correction and escalating Black Sea disruptions.” RESULTS OF OPERATIONS Three-month and nine-month periods ended September 30, 202612 During the three-month periods ended September 30, 2026 and 2025, the Company had an average of 29.5 and 35.5 vessels in its owned fleet and chartered in an average of 28.1 and 44.7 third-party owned dry bulk vessels, respectively. During the nine-month period ended September 30, 2026, the corresponding averages were 29.9 owned vessels and 25.0 chartered-in vessels. During the three-month period ended September 30, 2026, we sold the dry bulk vessel Bermondi with a DWT capacity of 55,469. During the three-month period ended September 30, 2025, we acquired and accepted delivery of the secondhand dry bulk vessels Imperator and Gorgo with an aggregate DWT capacity of 252,885, and we sold the dry bulk vessels Acuity, Verity, Bernis, Equity, Pythias and Gorgo with an aggregate DWT capacity of 281,897. During the nine-month period ended September 30, 2026, we took delivery of the dry bulk vessel Astros with a DWT capacity of 60,297 and we sold the dry bulk vessels Clara, Miracle and Bermondi with an aggregate DWT capacity of 292,669. During the three-month periods ended September 30, 2026 and 2025, owned-fleet ownership days totaled 2,716 and 3,270, respectively. During the nine-month period ended September 30, 2026, our owned-fleet ownership days totaled 8,173. Ownership days are one of the primary drivers of voyage revenue and vessels’ operating expenses and represent the aggregate number of days in a period during which each vessel in our fleet is owned. The decrease in Total voyage revenue and the improvement in Net Income in Q3 2026 vs Q3 2025 reflect, among other factors, the significant downsizing of the operating platform fleet following the agreement of the previously announced transaction (signed in the end of Q3 2025) with Cargill International S.A. (“Cargill”), together with actions taken to reduce the operating platform’s operating expenses. CONDENSED CASH FLOWS13 Net cash provided by operating activities during the three- and nine-month periods ended September 30, 2026 were $21.3 million and $41.5 million, respectively, and were principally affected by operating results, working-capital movements, dry-docking and special-survey expenditures, and interest payments. Net cash provided by investing activities during the three-month period ended September 30, 2026 was $14.8 million, principally reflecting the net proceeds from the sale of dry bulk vessel Bermondi and payments for vessels’ upgrades. Net cash provided by investing activities during the nine-month period ended September 30, 2026 was $32.0 million, which mainly include the net proceeds from the sales of the dry bulk vessels Clara, Miracle and Bermondi and payments for the acquisition of the dry bulk vessel Astros. Net cash used in financing activities during the nine-month period ended September 30, 2026 was $24.5 million, reflecting scheduled debt repayments and debt prepayment due to the sale of the dry bulk vessels Clara, Miracle and Bermondi. Debt-Free Vessels As of September 30, 2026, the Company had three debt-free vessels with an aggregate carrying capacity of 182,477 DWT. These unencumbered vessels, combined with the Company’s net cash position and the absence of near-term debt maturities, even prior to the completion of the refinancing of our existing indebtedness, provide additional financial flexibility. articles.summary: The SS United States has settled upright on the floor of the Gulf of Mexico, completing its transformation from record-breaking ocean liner to the world’s largest artificial reef. Early sonar...

Join the leading maritime news network Image courtesy SS United States: An Operational Guide to America's Flagship The SS United States has settled upright on the floor of the Gulf of Mexico, completing its transformation from record-breaking ocean liner to the world’s largest artificial reef. Early sonar and remotely operated vehicle inspections confirmed that the 990-foot vessel came to rest upright, just feet from its intended location, following its controlled sinking off Florida’s Gulf Coast on Wednesday, November 11. The first underwater images are also emerging. RV Explorer, a shipwreck research and salvage vessel based in Cape May, New Jersey, shared an image of diver Captain Will Hinton positioned in front of the ship’s stern. “Happy to report the SS United States is sitting perfectly upright,” RV Explorer said. The confirmation marks a significant milestone for a project that required extensive preparation to ensure the historic vessel would settle safely on the seabed and remain accessible to divers. According to Destin-Fort Walton Beach tourism officials, the ship now rests approximately 22 nautical miles offshore in about 180 feet of water, with its uppermost deck roughly 60 feet below the surface. The safety zone surrounding the deployment site has been lifted, allowing divers to begin exploring the wreck. “The successful deployment of the SS United States is a significant achievement, and I couldn’t be prouder of the team,” said Jennifer Adams, tourism director for Destin-Fort Walton Beach. “To see a vessel of this size come to rest upright, within feet of its intended location, is a great testament to the expertise and collaboration of everyone who helped bring this ambitious vision to life.” The SS United States was deliberately sunk on Veterans Day after weather concerns prompted Okaloosa County to move the operation forward from its original November 12 schedule. Hundreds of spectators gathered aboard nearby boats to witness the final moments of the ship that once held the title of the world’s fastest ocean liner. Crews opened intake valves to allow Gulf waters to flood the vessel in a controlled sinking operation. The ship gradually submerged before rolling to port and sinking below the surface, eventually settling onto the seabed. The deployment followed extensive work to prepare the former passenger liner for its new role, including environmental remediation and structural modifications designed to make the wreck safer for divers and marine life. The SS United States joins more than 580 artificial reef sites in the Destin-Fort Walton Beach area, although none comes close to matching its scale. “This sets Okaloosa County apart as a leader in the tourism industry worldwide and we could not be happier to see this project come to fruition,” said Okaloosa County Board Chairman Trey Goodwin. Beyond its significance as a diving attraction, the ship will become a large-scale marine research site. Scientists from the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, Dauphin Island Sea Lab and Louisiana State University will monitor biological, physical and chemical changes around the vessel as marine organisms begin colonizing its structure. Researchers hope the project will provide new insights into how artificial reefs develop over time and support marine ecosystems. “This is so much more than creating a new dive destination,” said Alex Fogg, natural resources chief for Destin-Fort Walton Beach. “It’s an opportunity to advance marine science on a scale we’ve never experienced before.” For the SS United States , the deployment marks another chapter in a remarkable history. Built in Newport News, Virginia, the liner entered service in 1952 and set a transatlantic speed record on her maiden voyage that remains unbeaten by any ocean liner. After retiring in 1969, she spent decades laid up, including a long period on the Philadelphia waterfront, as preservation efforts struggled to secure her future. Now, the former flagship has a permanent home beneath the Gulf. A future shoreside museum and visitor experience, being developed with the SS United States Conservancy, will preserve the ship’s history and artifacts for visitors who may never venture underwater. “Her legacy will live on,” said Conservancy Board Chair Susan Gibbs. The artificial reef project was funded through tourism revenue and contributions from project partners. articles.title: Euroports Rauma adopts Portchain Connect to improve berth planning
articles.summary: Euroports’ container terminal at the Port of Rauma in Finland is joining the Portchain Connect network to improve berth planning and coordination with shipping lines. The terminal will use the digital platform to exchange vessel schedules and operational information directly with carriers. The system will also allow...
articles.body: Euroports’ container terminal at the Port of Rauma in Finland is joining the Portchain Connect network to improve berth planning and coordination with shipping lines. The terminal will use the digital platform to exchange vessel schedules and operational information directly with carriers. The system will also allow both sides to agree on berthing arrangements through a shared digital process. Through Portchain Connect, Euroports Rauma will receive real-time updates on vessel schedules and container move counts. Terminal planners will then be able to respond to changes and propose alternative berthing times. The new system aims to improve communication between the terminal and its shipping line customers. It will also provide earlier access to operational data, allowing the terminal to adjust its berth plans more efficiently. “By implementing Portchain Connect, we are strengthening the way we coordinate vessel calls with our shipping line partners. Earlier access to reliable operational information helps us improve planning, respond more effectively to schedule changes, and continue delivering efficient and high-quality services to our customers,” said Tomi Rautio, Managing Director, Euroports Finland. Digital platform supports vessel coordination Portchain Connect enables container terminals and shipping lines to share schedule information through a single platform. It also supports digital agreements on berthing windows, reducing the need for manual communication. According to Portchain, the network connects more than 200 container terminals and six major container carriers. Together, these terminals represent more than 40% of global terminal capacity. The platform also provides live vessel tracking and terminal lineup information. These features are designed to improve schedule visibility and support Just-in-Time vessel operations. In addition, better coordination between terminals and carriers can help reduce vessel waiting times and support more efficient fuel consumption. Euroports Rauma operates at one of Finland’s main container ports and handles a wide range of cargo. Its operations include forest products, containers, fertilisers, minerals and project cargo. The Port of Rauma is Finland’s largest container port on the country’s west coast. The terminal also supports international trade through regular shipping connections with Europe, North Africa and North America. The new Portchain Connect implementation will support Euroports Rauma’s efforts to improve vessel planning and coordination with its shipping line partners.

articles.summary: By Lori-Ann LaRocco The Port of Los Angeles handled a record 1,026,872 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) in October, marking its second-busiest month ever and extending the strongest five-month cargo run...

By Lori-Ann LaRocco The Port of Los Angeles handled a record 1,026,872 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) in October, marking its second-busiest month ever and extending the strongest five-month cargo run in the port’s 118-year history. The October total followed September’s all-time record of 1,042,652 TEUs, marking the first time the nation’s busiest container port has surpassed 1 million units in consecutive months. Los Angeles has now crossed that threshold three times in 2026, another first. “On the heels of September’s all-time record, October makes it our second-best month ever,” said Port Executive Director Gene Seroka during a media briefing. “No other U.S. port has handled 1 million units in a single month, and we’ve now done it three times this year, including back-to-back months for the first time ever.” From June through October, the port processed nearly 5 million TEUs, its strongest five-month stretch on record. “What’s remarkable isn’t just the record volume but our ability to sustain this level of activity month after month,” Seroka said in a statement Thursday. Seroka attributed the historic cargo activity to continued consumer spending, retailers replenishing inventories, changes in trade policy and disruptions along other global shipping routes. Loaded imports reached 538,620 TEUs in October, up 25% from a year earlier and 30% above the port’s five-year October average. “This strength goes beyond holiday merchandise,” Seroka said. “We’re moving consumer goods alongside parts, components, and equipment destined for American businesses and manufacturers across the country.” The port also handled a record 373,271 empty TEUs, surpassing the previous monthly record set in September. Ocean carriers have been repositioning equipment to Asia to accommodate additional shipments. Exports, however, remain a weak spot. Loaded exports totaled 114,981 TEUs, down 7% from October 2025. “Exports have now declined year over year in six of the first 10 months here in 2026, as American farmers and manufacturers continue to face headwinds in overseas markets,” Seroka said. Through October, Los Angeles has handled 9,108,497 TEUs, 5% ahead of last year and 9% above its five-year average. Seroka said November volumes are also shaping up to be strong, raising the possibility of another annual record. “If December also delivers, I believe this could be the busiest year in our port’s 118-year history,” he said. Despite the historic volumes, a potential labor disruption and mounting rail delays threaten to complicate cargo movements at the neighboring ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach. The Pacific Maritime Association and International Longshore and Warehouse Union Local 26, which represents about 250 maritime watchmen at the ports, have extended contract negotiations through November 20 . The extension temporarily averts a walkout, but a strike remains possible if the two sides fail to reach an agreement. Although the watchmen represent a small portion of the waterfront workforce, a work stoppage could have a much broader impact. Other ILWU locals, including longshore workers in Local 13 and marine clerks in Local 63, have indicated they would honor Local 26 picket lines. A strike would come as both ports are already struggling with elevated intermodal container dwell times. Recent port data showed approximately 9,500 rail-bound import containers at Los Angeles had been waiting nine days or longer for on-dock rail transportation. At Long Beach, another 5,063 containers faced similar delays. Separate import dwell-time data from Los Angeles showed approximately 67% of containers moving through terminals within four days, while 11% remained five to eight days and 23% stayed nine days or longer. Logistics provider C.H. Robinson has identified a shortage of intermodal railcars in Southern California as a contributing factor to the slowdown. Trucking capacity is also under pressure. “Port congestion at LA and Long Beach due to increased import volume and reduced driver capacity continues to be highly elevated,” said Paul Brashier, vice president of global supply chain at ITS Logistics. “With congestion reducing the amount of containers a driver can execute daily, shippers should be prepared to add additional trucking capacity to navigate these conditions through Lunar New Year.” Any labor disruption could further extend container dwell times and create additional challenges for importers moving goods inland. Despite the operational pressures, Seroka remains optimistic about cargo demand heading into next year. After two visits to China and discussions with manufacturers, he said factories there are running at full capacity, with exporters anticipating strong shipments through the end of 2026 and into early 2027. The temporary easing of U.S.-China tariff tensions has provided some relief for shippers, while the extension of the suspension of U.S. port fees targeting Chinese vessels has removed another near-term source of uncertainty. Importers are also expected to accelerate shipments ahead of Lunar New Year, contributing to the elevated cargo flows. Still, the outlook remains vulnerable to further changes in trade policy, including potential Section 301 tariffs, the direction of U.S.-China negotiations and renewed tensions surrounding advanced semiconductor technology. There are also questions about how long American consumers can sustain the current pace of spending. High energy and food prices continue to pressure household budgets, while rising consumer debt raises additional questions about demand heading into 2027. The Federal Reserve Bank of New York recently reported that U.S. credit card balances reached a record $1.29 trillion in the third quarter. Another source of cargo demand—and uncertainty—is the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure. Trade data provider ImportGenius has been tracking shipments of data center components and infrastructure moving through Los Angeles and Long Beach as technology companies expand their computing capacity across the United States. But questions about future projects, electricity availability and the political environment could influence how much equipment continues to move through the ports. “The big players in the AI space have been competing largely on the capabilities of their models,” said Lynn Hughes, lead analyst for the trade research team at ImportGenius. “Recent election results and limited grid capacity will cause investors in data centers to re-evaluate their exposure. But it’s very likely that the next area of competition is efficiency in training and inference.” For now, the Port of Los Angeles is closing out 2026 with record cargo momentum and the prospect of its busiest year ever. Whether that pace can continue into 2027 will depend not only on consumer demand and U.S.-China trade relations, but also on the ability of Southern California’s ports, railroads and trucking networks to keep freight moving.
