Saronic has awarded a contract worth more than $100 million to Norway’s Syncrolift to design and supply what the companies say will be the world’s largest shiplift at its planned $3 billion Port Alpha shipyard in Brownsville, Texas. The system will feature a 300-meter (984-foot) lifting platform with a capacity of 67,000 metric tons, more than twice the lifting capacity of the next-largest installation, according to Saronic’s announcement Thursday. Syncrolift, a subsidiary of Oslo-listed Nekkar ASA, will manage the project from its headquarters near Oslo. The company previously disclosed the contract on November 4 without identifying the customer, calling it the largest order in its history. Final delivery is scheduled for 2028. The massive shiplift will play a central role in Saronic’s plans to rethink how ships are built, allowing multiple vessels to be assembled and outfitted simultaneously on land rather than occupying traditional dry docks. Instead of building ships in fixed docks, Port Alpha is being designed around a production system in which large hull sections are assembled and vessels move between workstations. The shiplift and accompanying transfer system will allow completed ships to be moved from their construction positions into the water. The tandem lifting system will incorporate condition-monitoring technology and digital-twin controls to monitor operations throughout the lifting process. “The scope and scale of this shiplift is foundational to how the yard will operate,” said Doug Lambert, Saronic’s co-founder and chief operating officer. The approach is intended to reduce bottlenecks associated with traditional shipbuilding, where dock availability and limited waterfront space can constrain production. By moving more construction and outfitting work onto land, Saronic aims to increase the number of vessels that can be built simultaneously. The contract marks another major step in the development of Port Alpha, which broke ground on September 30 . Located at the Port of Brownsville, the shipyard will initially occupy 835 acres, with the potential to expand to nearly 4,400 acres. Saronic plans to invest more than $3 billion in the project, which it says could eventually support up to 10,000 direct jobs. The facility is being developed to build both autonomous and crewed vessels for commercial and defense customers, reflecting growing efforts to expand U.S. shipbuilding capacity amid concerns over the country’s declining share of global ship production. According to Saronic’s Port Alpha development plans , the initial phase will accommodate ships measuring up to approximately 850 feet, with future expansion potentially supporting vessels exceeding 1,200 feet. The company is targeting initial operations in 2028, with plans to eventually produce as many as 20 ships annually by 2035. Its first vessels are expected to be Landing Craft Utility vessels under a U.S. Navy contract. Saronic is also working with South Korea’s Samsung Heavy Industries as it develops its shipbuilding capabilities. The Syncrolift agreement highlights the role international suppliers are expected to play in the project, even as Saronic positions Port Alpha as a major investment in rebuilding domestic maritime manufacturing capacity. The contract was announced in connection with the Atlantic Future Forum, a gathering of defense, security and technology leaders focused on cooperation among allied nations. articles.body: Dry Cargo Europe Seanergy lines up four more bulkers in $855m fleet push Adis Ajdin November 13, 2026 0 412 1 minute read Greek capesize specialist Seanergy Maritime has added four more vessels worth $264m to its fleet investment programme, taking its total spending commitments to $855m. The Nasdaq-listed owner, led by Stamatis Tsantanis, disclosed the latest acquisitions in its third-quarter update, with the deals covering two newbuildings and two secondhand bulkers, for arrivals between 2027 and 2029. The secondhand purchases comprise a 2019-built Japanese capesize of 180,000 dwt, to be renamed Midnightship , and a 2014-built Japanese newcastlemax of 210,000 dwt. On the newbuilding side, Seanergy has contracted a scrubber-fitted 210,000 dwt newcastlemax at China’s Hengli Shipbuilding and secured a scrubber-fitted 181,000 dwt capesize under construction in Japan. The latest additions expand Seanergy’s investment programme to 12 vessels — nine newbuildings and three secondhand ships — representing around 2.3m dwt of additional capacity. The owner has so far paid $127.4m towards the programme, leaving approximately $727.6m in commitments through 2029. Seanergy has also agreed the main terms of a $33m sale of the 2009-built capesize Friendship to spinoff United Maritime. The transaction, agreed in November, remains subject to lender approval and final documentation. Seanergy said it expects to release about $19.6m in net cash and record an accounting gain of $12.4m if completed. United, which has confirmed the purchase agreement separately, is continuing its shift towards larger bulkers. The company has also fixed its Squireship charter earnings for 2027 at more than $29,100 per day, following an earlier conversion of the Dukeship at over $35,000 per day. The two vessels now represent approximately $23.1m in contracted gross hire for next year. REUTERS/Stringer A projectile struck the engine room of the Liberia-flagged crude oil tanker Dominica Prosperity off the United Arab Emirates on Wednesday, forcing the evacuation of all 22 crew members as emergency crews battled a fire aboard the vessel. The attack was one of four tanker incidents documented in the latest maritime security advisory covering the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz, including a separate strike that left multiple seafarers injured. According to UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), the Dominica Prosperity was struck by an unidentified projectile at approximately 1800 UTC on November 11, about 14 nautical miles northwest of Ras Al Khaimah, UAE, near Mina Saqr. The projectile struck the tanker’s engine room. UKMTO said no casualties were reported and all crew members were safely evacuated. Firefighting operations were still underway when the warning was issued Thursday. India’s Minister of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Sarbananda Sonowal, identified the vessel as the Dominica Prosperity and confirmed that 19 Indian nationals were among the 22 crew members rescued by the UAE Coast Guard. Sonowal said the tanker had been drifting off Mina Saqr when it was targeted. “The entire 22-member crew was swiftly and safely evacuated by the UAE Coast Guard and all 19 of our Indian nationals are completely safe with no injuries,” Sonowal wrote on X. He added that Indian authorities remained in contact with the vessel’s management company to coordinate support for the crew. Reuters reported that the tanker is operated by South Korea’s Sinokor Maritime Co., citing maritime risk information provider MARISKS. Maritime security company Ambrey said the vessel was struck near its stern as it exited the Strait of Hormuz. The extent of the vessel’s damage and any potential environmental impact is unknown. Multiple Tankers Struck in Separate Attacks The Dominica Prosperity incident comes amid a series of attacks on commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz. In its November 12 advisory update, the Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) documented four tanker attacks since its previous report, including two in the Persian Gulf and two in the Strait of Hormuz. One of the incidents involved the tanker Fujairah Energy , which was struck by an unknown projectile while traveling eastbound in the Arabian Gulf on November 10. UKMTO said multiple crew members were injured and taken ashore for medical treatment. The remaining crew were reported safe and accounted for. No damage assessment or information about possible environmental impacts was immediately available. Another tanker, identified in the JMIC advisory as NCC Fajr, was struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz on November 11. Omani authorities reported the attack at approximately 0200 UTC north of Khasab, Oman. UKMTO initially reported the incident without confirming a strike but subsequently reclassified it as an attack after receiving confirmation that the vessel had been hit. All crew members were reported safe. The fourth incident involved an unidentified tanker struck by an unknown projectile on November 10, approximately 19 nautical miles northeast of Lima, Oman, in the Strait of Hormuz. The crew was reported safe, with no environmental damage reported. The four incidents were separately documented by JMIC, although several were disclosed only after the attacks occurred. Maritime Security Threat Remains Severe JMIC said the latest attacks bring the number of recorded maritime security incidents since March 1 to 181, underscoring the continuing dangers facing commercial vessels operating in the region. JMIC attributed the continuing threat to Iranian attacks and harassment, including drone overflights, surveillance of merchant vessels and radio communications directed at ships. However, the perpetrators of the four latest projectile attacks have not been individually established in the UKMTO warnings. Commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains well below pre-conflict levels. According to JMIC, independent tracking data showed single-digit to low-double-digit vessel transits per day, while U.S. Naval Cooperation and Guidance for Shipping (NCAGS) figures indicated approximately 34 U.S.-assisted transits per day over the latest 96-hour reporting period. The two figures reflect different reporting methods and should not be treated as directly comparable measures of total traffic. The advisory also pointed to persistent congestion at anchorages near the Strait. JMIC estimated approximately 211 commercial vessels were stationary at major anchorages east of Hormuz, including Fujairah, Khor Fakkan, Sohar and Musandam. The attacks come as commercial shipping continues to navigate the dangers posed by the conflict involving Iran, the United States and Israel, with both military operations and maritime security threats complicating vessel movements through one of the world’s most important oil shipping routes. UKMTO has advised vessels operating in the region to exercise caution and report suspicious activity while authorities investigate the latest incidents. articles.title: HHLA container throughput falls 7.3% as automation challenges weigh on earnings
articles.summary: Hamburger Hafen und Logistik AG (HHLA) reported a 7.3% decline in container throughput during the first nine months of 2026, as terminal automation projects and operational disruptions affected performance at its Hamburg facilities. Total container throughput fell to 4.45 million TEUs, compared with 4.80 million TEUs...
articles.body: Hamburger Hafen und Logistik AG (HHLA) reported a 7.3% decline in container throughput during the first nine months of 2026, as terminal automation projects and operational disruptions affected performance at its Hamburg facilities. Total container throughput fell to 4.45 million TEUs, compared with 4.80 million TEUs in the same period last year. Meanwhile, container transport volumes increased slightly by 0.5% to 1.51 million TEUs. Despite lower handling volumes, Group revenue rose by 3.3% to €1.38 billion. However, operating profit (EBIT) declined by 30.7% to €81.2 million, down from €117.1 million a year earlier. According to HHLA, the implementation of additional automation at its Hamburg terminals affected productivity. Strike-related disruptions in the third quarter, severe winter weather and changing international trade flows also contributed to the decline. “We have made good progress with our transformation agenda, but operationally we are not yet where we want to be. Our focus is therefore clearly on stabilising automated processes and significantly improving the quality of handling operations,” said Jeroen Eijsink, CEO, HHLA. Hamburg terminals face operational pressure Container throughput at HHLA’s Hamburg terminals decreased by 7.7% to 4.20 million TEUs, compared with 4.55 million TEUs in the previous year. At the company’s international terminals, volumes declined by 1.6% to 246,000 TEUs. HHLA attributed the decrease to weaker economic conditions in Estonia and changes in Mediterranean shipping routes linked to geopolitical tensions. The security situation also affected operations at its CTO terminal, where throughput almost came to a standstill during the third quarter. In the Container segment, revenue declined slightly by 0.7% to €637.2 million. Additional storage income from longer container dwell times helped offset part of the reduction in handling volumes. However, operating profit in the segment fell sharply by 51.3% to €29.4 million. The operating margin also decreased to 4.6%, compared with 9.4% a year earlier. Higher personnel and energy costs, alongside productivity restrictions during the automation process, placed further pressure on earnings. Intermodal business records modest growth HHLA’s Intermodal segment delivered a more stable performance during the reporting period, supported by slightly higher transport volumes and increased average revenues. Rail transport volumes rose by 0.6% to 1.31 million TEUs, driven mainly by traffic with North German seaports and connections to Poland. Road transport volumes remained unchanged at 201,000 TEUs. Intermodal revenue increased by 7.8% to €651 million, while operating profit rose by 2.3% to €78 million. Nevertheless, construction work along major transport routes and capacity constraints at North German ports continued to affect operations. Separately, HHLA recorded non-cash impairment charges of €21.4 million in its Logistics segment following a review of its investment portfolio. These included €12 million related to HHLA Sky and €9.4 million linked to omoqo. The company had already revised its full-year earnings outlook in October, reflecting weaker container handling volumes and operational challenges. HHLA now expects Group EBIT of between €115 million and €135 million for 2026, compared with its previous forecast of €150 million to €170 million.
takeaways: Total container throughput fell to 4.45 million TEUs, compared with 4.80 million TEUs in the same period last year.
Meanwhile, container transport volumes increased slightly by 0.5% to 1.51 million TEUs.
Despite lower handling volumes, Group revenue rose by 3.3% to €1.38 billion.

articles.title: Wind-Powered Cargo Ship Neoliner Origin Cuts Fuel Consumption 70% in First Year
articles.summary: French shipping company Neoline says its wind-powered cargo vessel Neoliner Origin has delivered fuel savings of up to 70% during its first year of commercial service, offering an early test...

Join the leading maritime news network Photo Courtesy NEOLINE French shipping company Neoline says its wind-powered cargo vessel Neoliner Origin has delivered fuel savings of up to 70% during its first year of commercial service, offering an early test of whether wind propulsion can deliver substantial emissions reductions in transatlantic shipping. The 136-meter roll-on/roll-off cargo ship, which entered service in October 2025 , completed nine commercial round trips between Europe and North America, covering more than 62,000 nautical miles and carrying over 12,000 tonnes of cargo. According to first-year operating results released by Neoline, the vessel reduced fuel consumption by an average of 66% over its first year compared with conventional vessels using the Global Logistics Emissions Council (GLEC) fleet reference. Savings reached 70% when considering 2026 operations alone. The company estimates the vessel saved 3,502 tonnes of fuel over the full period, avoiding approximately 11,228 tonnes of CO2 emissions compared with the reference. The Return of Sail Power: Cargo Ships Are Turning Back to the Wind A separate analysis comparing Neoliner Origin with a simulated conventional vessel operating the same routes at 15 knots found fuel savings ranging from 62% to 67%, although Neoline acknowledged methodological uncertainty in the simulations. The results come as shipowners increasingly explore wind propulsion as a way to reduce fuel consumption and emissions without relying entirely on alternative fuels or new bunkering infrastructure. Unlike conventional cargo ships fitted with wind-assist technology, Neoliner Origin was designed from the outset to use wind as its primary means of propulsion, with its SolidSail system providing much of the power needed for transatlantic crossings. Technical Challenges Remain Despite the fuel savings, Neoline acknowledged that technical problems with the vessel’s sail system limited its performance during the first year. The company said issues affecting the sails significantly reduced the time the vessel could operate under full sail, preventing it from realizing the system’s full potential. When fully operational, however, Neoliner Origin has regularly exceeded 15 knots under sail alone. In June 2026, the vessel reached a peak speed through the water of 16.6 knots with its engine stopped. Neoline is working with French shipbuilder Chantiers de l’Atlantique to address the problems, with a maintenance period scheduled for February 2027 to restore full use of the SolidSail rig. The company is now targeting fuel savings of at least 78% against the GLEC fleet reference, with hopes of approaching or exceeding 80% during 2027. “This first year of operations confirms the potential of wind propulsion to significantly reduce fuel consumption and CO2 emissions in maritime transport,” said Jean Zanuttini, chairman and CEO of Neoline. “It has also been challenging, as can be expected when developing a prototype vessel, and has enabled us to draw valuable lessons to improve its performance.” Commercial Service Expands Beyond its environmental performance, the first year provided an opportunity to test the commercial viability of a wind-powered cargo service operating on a regular transatlantic schedule. Neoliner Origin transported 1,845 cargo units totaling approximately 12,063 tonnes and nearly 56,000 cubic meters. Cargoes included vehicles, containers, oversized industrial equipment, machinery and refrigerated goods. The vessel operates between Montoir-de-Bretagne in France and North America, with calls at Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon, Baltimore and Halifax. In September, Neoline expanded the service with a new call at Zeebrugge, Belgium, providing additional access to European automotive, ro-ro and project cargo markets. Neoline also reported developing commercial partnerships with CMA CGM and CEVA, while expanding its North American relationships, including with Canadian partner Montship. The ship carried more than 170 passengers during its first year, reflecting another element of Neoline’s business model, which combines freight transportation with passenger crossings. The results offer an early indication of what wind propulsion can achieve in commercial shipping, although the vessel’s technical challenges also highlight the difficulties of bringing the technology into regular service. For Neoline, the next test will be whether improvements to the sail system can deliver more consistent performance while maintaining reliable cargo operations. “We are confident in our ability to approach, and potentially exceed, 80% fuel savings as early as 2027,” Zanuttini said. articles.title: MSC raises December FAK rates to Mediterranean and Black Sea
articles.summary: MSC has announced higher Freight All Kinds (FAK) rates for shipments from the Far East to the Mediterranean, North Africa and the Black Sea, effective from 1 December 2026, while maintaining its existing rates to Northern Europe. articles.body: MSC has announced higher Freight All Kinds (FAK) rates for shipments from the Far East to the Mediterranean, North Africa and the Black Sea, effective from 1 December 2026, while maintaining its existing rates to Northern Europe. The new tariffs will remain in effect until further notice, but no later than 14 December 2026. They cover shipments from all Far East ports, including Japan, South Korea and Southeast Asia, to destinations across Northern Europe, the Western and Eastern Mediterranean, the Adriatic, North Africa and the Black Sea. Compared with the carrier’s rates for the second half of November, the new tariffs represent increases across most destinations. For 40-foot dry and high-cube containers, rates to the Western Mediterranean and Adriatic will rise by US$1,200 to US$6,500, while those to the Eastern Mediterranean will increase by US$800 to the same level. Black Sea rates will also increase by US$800, reaching US$6,700 per 40-foot container. Northern European rates will remain unchanged at US$4,600. New MSC freight rates from 1 December The announced FAK rates, expressed in US dollars, are as follows: Destination 20-foot dry 40-foot dry/HC North Europe 3,220 4,600 West Mediterranean 5,100 6,500 Adriatic 5,100 6,500 East Mediterranean 5,100 6,500 Black Sea 5,200 6,700 Algeria 6,100 8,200 Libya 6,000 8,000 Morocco (Casablanca) 5,500 7,000 Tunisia 6,000 8,000 North African destinations will continue to carry the highest published rates. Algeria will reach US$8,200 per 40-foot container, an increase of US$600 from the second half of November, while rates to Libya and Tunisia will each rise by US$800 to US$8,000. Morocco’s Casablanca rate will also increase by US$800, reaching US$7,000 per 40-foot container. Additional surcharges and conditions MSC stated that the announced rates apply from base port to base port, with shipments involving out-ports subject to the usual Transport Additional Origin and Destination (TAO/TAD) charges. The published FAK rates already include the ocean freight component and a Global Fuel Surcharge (GFS) of US$304 per TEU for December, compared with US$266 per TEU in November. They also incorporate an Emission Control Area (ECA) surcharge of US$15 per TEU for Mediterranean destinations and specified Northern European countries, or US$52 per TEU for other Nordic and Baltic destinations. Additional charges include a Carbon Limitation Surcharge (CLS) of US$20 per TEU and a Carbon Review Surcharge (CRS) of US$90 per TEU for Northern Europe and US$133 per TEU for the Mediterranean. Piracy Risk Surcharge (PRS) and Suez Canal Surcharge (SCS) provisions also apply according to MSC’s separate announcement dated 4 November 2026. The carrier noted that its FAK rates exclude IMO-classified commodities and high-value cargo. Terminal handling charges and other applicable costs may also be added. The announced figures represent MSC’s published tariffs for the specified period rather than confirmed transaction rates paid by shippers.

articles.title: Konecranes secures mobile harbor crane order for Peru’s Port of Matarani
articles.summary: Konecranes has received an order from Terminal Internacional del Sur (Tisur) for a new mobile harbor crane at the Port of Matarani in southern Peru. articles.body: Konecranes has received an order from Terminal Internacional del Sur (Tisur) for a new mobile harbor crane at the Port of Matarani in southern Peru. The order marks the company’s first sale of a factory-new mobile harbor crane in Peru. The agreement covers one Konecranes Gottwald ESP.6 Mobile Harbor Crane. It was recorded in the third quarter of 2026, while the equipment is expected to enter operation by the end of March 2027. The investment forms part of Tisur’s US$598 million port modernisation programme. The new crane will handle containers, general cargo and project cargo at the multipurpose terminal. It will have a maximum lifting capacity of 125 tonnes. Tisur already operates a pre-owned Konecranes Gottwald crane manufactured in the 1990s. The operator’s experience with this equipment played a role in its decision to purchase the new model. “Our existing crane has proven its reliability over many years. We wanted to build on that experience with a new, high-performance crane to support our ambitious plans for the port. The excellent advice and strong local service support from Konecranes were also key factors in our decision,” said Mauricio Nuñez del Prado, General Manager, Tisur. Hybrid technology supports port operations The new crane will use a hybrid drive system with capacitors to reduce energy consumption and emissions. Its design will also allow a future conversion to fully electric operation. In addition, Tisur has selected a motor grab for bulk cargo handling. This will allow the crane to support different types of cargo at the terminal. “We’re delighted to break new ground in Peru together with Tisur. Our relationship with them demonstrates the value of working closely with customers over the long term, supported by reliable equipment and a strong local service network,” said Alfredo Canibano, Regional Sales Manager, Konecranes Port Solutions. The order adds new cargo-handling equipment to the Port of Matarani as Tisur continues its wider modernisation programme.

articles.title: New ultra-deep oil & gas discovery marks ‘major breakthrough’ in Bohai Sea
articles.summary: CNOOC has revealed an ultra-deep natural gas find in the central Bohai Sea, with a high-yield volcanic well testing at 800,000 cubic meters per day.
articles.body: Exploration & Production November 12, 2026 · 1 minute ago New ultra-deep oil & gas discovery marks ‘major breakthrough’ in Bohai Sea CNOOC has revealed an ultra-deep natural gas find in the central Bohai Sea, with a high-yield volcanic well testing at 800,000 cubic meters per day. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Offshore platform (for illustration purposes) Source: CNOOC Chinese state-owned oil and gas giant China National Offshore Oil Corporation (CNOOC) has made a high-yield natural gas discovery in volcanic rock more than 5,700 meters beneath the central Bohai Sea, opening doors to a new frontier for ultra-deep exploration in the region and bringing the company one step closer to building a trillion-cubic-meter gas province off the coast of China. CNOOC has drilled a high-yield volcanic oil and gas well in ultra-deep formations over 5,000 meters deep in Bohai, said to represent a major breakthrough in ultra-deep natural gas exploration offshore China. The well, which is adjacent to the Bozhong Sag , the largest hydrocarbon-rich sag in Bohai, encountered a cumulative total of over 120 meters of gas pay zone in volcanic formations and was completed at a depth of 5,770 meters. The well was tested to produce approximately 800,000 cubic meters (around 28 million cubic feet) per day of natural gas, uncovering promising exploration prospects in the offshore ultra-deep volcanic rocks and promoting the natural gas exploration process in the Bozhong Sag. " In recent years, CNOOC Limited has continued to strengthen theoretical innovation in deep and ultra-deep oil and gas enrichment in basins with high heat flow and strong activity, and to intensify research on key technologies. Exploration in China’s offshore areas has achieved a major leap from shallow to deep and ultra-deep formations. The success of this well has opened up a new play for offshore ultra-deep natural gas exploration and expanded the scope of deep oil and gas exploration in Bohai. It is of positive significance for accelerating the ultra-deep exploration process in Bohai and for building a major gas province of one trillion cubic meters in Bohai. articles.summary: Singapore has retained its position as the world’s leading maritime hub, while Shanghai has climbed to second place and Asia now accounts for three of the world’s five highest-ranked maritime...

Join the leading maritime news network File Photo of Singapore Anchorage: anek.soowannaphoom/Shutterstock Singapore has retained its position as the world’s leading maritime hub, while Shanghai has climbed to second place and Asia now accounts for three of the world’s five highest-ranked maritime cities, according to a new report from DNV and Menon Economics. The Leading Maritime Cities 2026 report, released Thursday, ranks Singapore first overall, followed by Shanghai, London, Rotterdam and Tokyo. Singapore has held the top position since the report was first published in 2015, maintaining its lead through a combination of shipping activity, port infrastructure, maritime services and investment in technology. The biggest shift in this year’s rankings came from Shanghai, which climbed from fourth to second place, overtaking both Rotterdam and London. Tokyo also returned to the top five, replacing Oslo, which ranked fifth in 2024. The results mark a shift toward Asia, which now accounts for three of the top five maritime cities, compared with two in the previous edition. Singapore ranked first in three of the report’s five categories: Shipping, Ports and Logistics, and Attractiveness and Competitiveness. It also placed third in Maritime Finance and Law and fourth in Maritime Technology. Its position reflects the concentration of shipowners and fleet managers operating in the city-state, alongside one of the world’s most important ports, extensive liner shipping connections and growing capabilities in alternative-fuel bunkering. “This has been a year of disruption and adjustment for the maritime industry,” said Cristina Saenz de Santa Maria, CEO Maritime at DNV. “Faced with these challenges, the leading maritime cities have demonstrated that leadership is built not on a single activity, but on breadth.” While Singapore maintained its lead, the report highlights how different maritime centers are competing through their respective strengths. Shanghai’s rise underscores the growing influence of Asian maritime hubs, while London and Rotterdam remain among the world’s leading centers for maritime business, services and port-related activity. North American maritime hubs lost ground in the latest rankings. New York remained the region’s highest-ranked city but slipped from sixth to eighth place globally. Houston fell five positions to 20th, while Los Angeles dropped from 19th to 25th. Vancouver, Canada recorded an even steeper decline, falling from 13th to 28th place. The changes come as Asian maritime centers gain ground in the rankings, although DNV and Menon Economics caution that methodological updates in the 2026 report may affect comparisons with previous editions. The report also points to Dubai as a city to watch. In a survey of maritime industry experts looking ahead five years, Dubai ranked third among the cities expected to lead the global maritime sector. “This year, that points to a shift in the balance of maritime power. Asia now holds three of the top five places, up from two in 2024,” said Erik Jakobsen, partner and chair of Menon Economics. “At the same time, established European hubs such as London and Rotterdam continue to demonstrate the importance of strong maritime services and port-industrial clusters.” The rankings are based on an assessment of 50 maritime cities across five categories: Shipping, Maritime Finance and Law, Maritime Technology, Ports and Logistics, and Attractiveness and Competitiveness. Researchers initially screened more than 15,000 cities using maritime industry data before selecting 50 for a more detailed evaluation. The final assessment uses 48 indicators and incorporates responses from more than 200 maritime industry experts worldwide. Now in its seventh edition, the report has expanded its methodology to account for changes reshaping the maritime industry, including the energy transition, technological development, workforce availability and resilience. DNV and Menon Economics caution that changes in rankings should be viewed in the context of those methodological updates, which can affect comparisons with previous editions. The findings also suggest that maritime competitiveness increasingly depends on more than fleet ownership or cargo volumes alone. “Cities compete from different positions, and their strengths reflect the role they play in the global maritime industry,” said Shahrin Osman, global business development leader for maritime advisory at DNV and co-author of the report. “Those that come out on top link infrastructure, commercial decision-making, specialist services, technology and talent into a single working cluster.” For Singapore, that combination has been enough to keep it at the top of the rankings for more than a decade, even as competition among the world’s leading maritime centers intensifies. articles.title: GEODIS launches new rail freight connection between Italy and France
articles.summary: GEODIS has launched a new rail freight service connecting Vicenza in northern Italy with Noisy-le-Sec, near Paris. The new route expands the company’s European intermodal network and provides another transport option for businesses in Italy’s Veneto region. The first train departed on 19 October 2026, marking the...
articles.body: GEODIS has launched a new rail freight service connecting Vicenza in northern Italy with Noisy-le-Sec, near Paris. The new route expands the company’s European intermodal network and provides another transport option for businesses in Italy’s Veneto region. The first train departed on 19 October 2026, marking the start of the service operated by Captrain and Hexafret. Both companies belong to Rail Logistics Europe, part of the SNCF Group alongside GEODIS. Initially, the service offers one departure per week in each direction. However, GEODIS plans to increase the frequency to two weekly departures per direction from January 2027. The connection is designed to transport several types of freight, including packaged liquid and powder goods. It also extends the company’s existing rail services in northern Italy, which already cover Lombardy, Piedmont and Emilia-Romagna through its Novara connection. New service targets intermodal freight growth According to GEODIS, the new rail connection can reduce CO₂ emissions per shipment by an average of 80% compared with diesel-powered road transport. The estimate includes road transport before and after the rail journey, while actual savings depend on operating conditions. The company based its emissions comparison on EcoTransIT World calculations. In addition, the service can carry up to 28 tonnes of goods per transport unit, compared with the 25 tonnes typically transported by road. GEODIS aims to reach an annual volume of 6,500 swap bodies by 2027. The planned increase in service frequency will support this target as the company expands its intermodal transport activities. The company also expects the rail connection to offer greater cost stability compared with road-only transport, particularly during periods of fluctuating fuel prices. “With the Vicenza-Paris connection, we are expanding our intermodal offer and introducing a new railway axis to serve companies in the North East of Italy,” said Marc Vollet, EVP European Road Network, GEODIS. The route strengthens the company’s existing freight network between France and Italy. It also provides businesses in northeastern Italy with a direct rail connection to the Paris region. Captrain and Hexafret will provide rail transport services for the new connection, drawing on their existing European operations. The service enters operation against a backdrop of significant trade flows between the two countries. According to GEODIS, bilateral trade in goods and services reached €136 billion in 2025. Italy ranks as France’s fourth-largest trading partner, while France is Italy’s second-largest. Around 4,000 companies operate across both markets, supporting demand for cross-border freight transport. The latest connection forms part of GEODIS’ wider strategy to expand intermodal services and provide lower-emission alternatives to long-distance road transport.

articles.title: Farewell to America’s Flagship: SS United States Sinks After 74 Years
articles.summary: The legendary ocean liner, which still holds the transatlantic speed record, took hours to sink off Florida’s Gulf Coast, ending a remarkable chapter in American maritime history. The SS United...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Crews prepare to sink the former ocean liner SS United States to create an artificial reef about 22 miles off the coast of Destin, Florida, US, November 11, 2026. Tony Giberson/USA Today Network via REUTERS. The legendary ocean liner, which still holds the transatlantic speed record, took hours to sink off Florida’s Gulf Coast, ending a remarkable chapter in American maritime history. The SS United States , the fastest ocean liner ever built and one of the last great symbols of America’s maritime golden age, sank off Florida’s Gulf Coast Wednesday night, November 11, bringing a 74-year journey to an end. The 990-foot vessel disappeared beneath the Gulf around 9 p.m. Central Time, following an hours-long controlled sinking operation approximately 22 nautical miles southwest of Destin-Fort Walton Beach. The ship, once celebrated as America’s Flagship, will now begin a new chapter as what officials describe as the world’s largest artificial reef. But the grand old liner did not go down easily. Despite extensive preparations to allow seawater to flood the ship, the sinking took considerably longer than initially anticipated. As darkness fell, the SS United States remained stubbornly afloat, slowly settling deeper into the water. In her final moments, video showed the vessel descending stern-first, her bow rising sharply as she rolled to port before disappearing beneath the surface. After several hours, the SS United States, an ocean liner, is intentionally sunk off the coast of Florida to become the world's largest artificial reef. pic.twitter.com/DwvU2Njf0f The dramatic finish raised questions about whether the ship would settle upright on the seabed as intended. Subsequent reports indicated that she had landed upright, although confirmation of her final position through an underwater survey remained important. UPDATE (Nov. 12, 2026): The SS United States has been confirmed sitting upright on the Gulf of Mexico seafloor. Early inspections show the vessel settled within feet of its intended location, and the safety zone has been lifted, allowing divers to access the world’s largest artificial reef. The operation was overseen by Coleen Marine, a contractor specializing in end-of-life vessel services. Unlike sinkings that use explosives to rapidly open a hull, the SS United States was sent down through controlled flooding. Crews had removed hundreds of portholes, cut openings between decks and prepared internal spaces to allow seawater to enter. The approach was intended to produce a controlled descent, but the size and structure of the ship made the process challenging. For generations of mariners and ocean liner enthusiasts, the sinking marked a bittersweet farewell to a vessel that once represented the height of American passenger shipping. The SS United States was the vision of legendary naval architect William Francis Gibbs, who spent much of his career pursuing the dream of building an American ocean liner capable of outperforming Europe’s finest ships. Built by Newport News Shipbuilding in Virginia for United States Lines, the ship entered service in 1952 as a technological marvel. At 990 feet long, she was longer than the RMS Titanic , powered by steam turbines developing approximately 240,000 shaft horsepower, and designed with an extraordinary emphasis on speed, lightweight construction and fire safety. Her design also reflected the strategic realities of the early Cold War. Developed with federal support, the vessel was intended to serve as both a luxury passenger liner and, if needed, a high-speed military troop transport. But it was her maiden voyage that secured her place in maritime history. In July 1952, the SS United States crossed the Atlantic in just three days, 10 hours and 40 minutes, averaging 35.59 knots and capturing the coveted Blue Riband from Britain’s RMS Queen Mary . More than seven decades later, her west-to-east transatlantic speed record remains unbroken by an ocean liner. The ship quickly became a national showpiece, carrying presidents, celebrities, business leaders and thousands of ordinary passengers between the United States and Europe. Grace Kelly, Elizabeth Taylor and John F. Kennedy were among her famous passengers. For nearly two decades, her distinctive red, white and blue funnels were an unmistakable presence on the North Atlantic. Despite her extraordinary speed and prestige, the SS United States could not escape the transformation of transatlantic travel. The rise of commercial aviation steadily eroded demand for passenger liners, making it increasingly difficult to justify the enormous cost of operating a ship built for speed. In November 1969, after approximately 800 transatlantic crossings, the SS United States was withdrawn from service. She would never carry paying passengers again. What followed was a succession of ownership changes, failed redevelopment proposals and long periods of inactivity. The ship spent years laid up in Virginia before eventually arriving in Philadelphia in 1996. There, she remained for nearly three decades, her once-proud hull gradually deteriorating along the Delaware River. Although her engines had fallen silent and much of her original interior had been removed, the vessel continued to inspire a passionate preservation movement. The nonprofit SS United States Conservancy, led for years by Susan Gibbs, granddaughter of the ship’s designer, worked to secure a permanent future for the liner. Various proposals envisioned converting her into a floating hotel, museum, entertainment complex or waterfront attraction. None ultimately succeeded. As gCaptain reported in June 2024 , a legal battle over pier fees and the ship’s longtime berth brought preservation efforts to a crisis. A federal court ruling requiring the vessel to leave Philadelphia forced her owners to confront an increasingly difficult reality: without a viable redevelopment project or another place to dock, the ship faced the prospect of being scrapped. In October 2024, ownership of the SS United States was transferred to Okaloosa County, Florida, under an agreement to transform the historic liner into an artificial reef. The decision offered an alternative to demolition, but it also meant abandoning the longstanding dream of preserving the entire ship above water. On February 19, 2025, the SS United States departed Philadelphia under tow , passing down the Delaware River and leaving behind the city that had been her home for nearly 30 years. She arrived in Mobile, Alabama, the following month, where contractors began the extensive process of preparing the vessel for deployment. According to Okaloosa County, all 128 fuel and lubricant tanks were emptied and cleaned, environmental remediation was carried out across her 12 decks, and hundreds of historic objects and components were removed for preservation. Among the items saved were the vessel’s iconic funnels, radar mast and other artifacts intended for a future land-based museum dedicated to her history. The project faced a last-minute legal challenge from preservation advocates raising environmental concerns, but an emergency request to halt the sinking was denied. On November 9, the SS United States left Mobile under tow for the last leg of her journey. Unlike her celebrated Atlantic crossings, there were no passengers aboard, no record to chase and no port of arrival. Her destination was the ocean floor. For those who spent years fighting to save the ship, Wednesday’s sinking was an especially painful moment. In a statement issued after the sinking , the SS United States Preservation Foundation, which had opposed the reefing project, paid tribute to the vessel and the generations of Americans who built, operated and fought to preserve her. The foundation described the ship as an achievement of American industry and engineering, born from the vision of brothers William Francis and Frederic Herbert Gibbs and constructed by American shipbuilders, including veterans of World War II. For more than a year, the group had pursued efforts to prevent the sinking, appealing to elected officials, raising environmental concerns and seeking alternatives that would preserve the vessel above water. “We believed then, as we believe now, that a nation should preserve the greatest achievements of those who came before us, not merely remember them after they are gone,” the foundation said. Despite losing its fight to save the ship, the organization pledged to continue preserving her history and honoring those who built and sailed aboard her. “You deserved a different ending, and will never be forgotten,” the foundation said in its farewell. The statement underscored the divide surrounding the ship’s fate. While Okaloosa County and supporters of the artificial reef project see the sinking as a way to give the vessel a new purpose, preservationists regard it as the irreversible loss of an irreplaceable piece of American maritime heritage. The ship’s sinking on Veterans Day carried an additional historical resonance. Although she was never called upon to serve as a troop transport, her design was closely tied to America’s national defense during the Cold War. The SS United States now rests in approximately 180 feet of water, where she is expected to attract marine life, divers and recreational fishermen, creating a major new attraction along Florida’s Emerald Coast. The project will also provide a research opportunity. Scientists from the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution plan to study how marine organisms colonize the massive steel structure and how an artificial reef ecosystem develops over time. The sinking remains controversial among those who had hoped the ship could survive as a museum or waterfront landmark. Others see the artificial reef as a more dignified outcome than dismantling her for scrap. Both views reflect the extraordinary attachment the vessel inspired long after she ceased to be commercially useful. The SS United States was built during an era when national prestige could be measured by the speed, size and sophistication of a country’s merchant fleet. She was a product of American shipyards, American engineering and a belief that the nation’s merchant marine could compete with the world’s best. Today, no American-flagged ocean liner makes the regularly scheduled transatlantic crossings that once defined her career. Her sinking marks the physical end of that history above the waterline. But the achievement she represented remains. For 74 years, no ocean liner has surpassed the transatlantic speed record she established on her maiden voyage. The ship that once raced across the Atlantic faster than any ocean liner before or since now rests beneath the Gulf, her days of crossing oceans finally over. The SS United States will never sail again, but her record—and her place in American maritime history—will endure. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Artist’s impression of Nordion Energi’s biogas liquefaction plant at the Port of Gothenburg Source: Port of Gothenburg The Port of Gothenburg, which is perceived as the largest port in the Nordic countries, has tucked a new green transition milestone under its belt with the installation of a 500-cubic-meter storage tank for liquefied biogas (LBG). Built and owned by Nordion Energi and scheduled to open in the second quarter of 2027, Sweden's first grid-connected biogas liquefaction plant is set to unlock large-scale renewable bunkering for the shipping industry and supercharge the local green fuel value chain. The construction milestone for the biogas liquefaction plant at the Port of Gothenburg comes as the facility’s storage tank for LBG got installed. This renewable fuel with low climate impact is said to have the ability to replace fossil alternatives in several sectors. As a result, the interest in the fuel is growing rapidly, particularly in shipping. " Shipping’s transition requires a collaborative value chain. This facility strengthens the port’s position in renewable bunker fuels and makes it possible to offer LBG to the shipping sector on a larger scale. As we see more and more vessels on order for LBG operation, we also see strong potential for increased bunkering at the Port of Gothenburg. " — Therese Jällbrink Head of Renewable Energy at the Port of Gothenburg According to the Port of Gothenburg, groundworks, including foundations and base slabs, have been completed, and the LBG tank is the first of the plant’s key components to be installed. The tank, which arrived at the European port by vessel, has a volume of 500 cubic meters and weighs close to 140 tonnes. It will be able to store up to 200 tonnes of LBG once the facility is operational. articles.body: Americas Environment Operations Tech US ethanol industry eyes growing marine fuel market Bojan Lepic November 12, 2026 0 422 1 minute read WinGD WinGD Ethanol could emerge as an alternative marine fuel for the growing fleet of methanol-capable ships, with existing engines and bunkering infrastructure requiring only limited modifications, according to a new industry study. The report, Marine Ethanol: Unlocking the US Opportunity , published by the Maritime Ethanol & Methanol Alliance (MEMA), says the fuel could support more than 300 methanol-capable vessels currently operating or on order, either independently or blended with methanol. The study identifies the US as a potential major supplier, with annual ethanol production capacity of 18.5bn gallons compared with 16.4bn gallons in 2025, leaving about 2bn gallons of spare capacity. According to the report, supplying just 1% of shipping’s annual fuel consumption would require around 1bn gallons of ethanol. Increasing that share to 5% by the mid-2030s would require approximately 5bn gallons. The findings follow Maersk’s first commercial ship-to-ship bunkering of US-produced corn ethanol aboard its dual-fuel containership Tangier Maersk in Houston in September. The study also highlights potential environmental benefits, estimating reductions of 40% to 94% in nitrogen oxide emissions and 90% to 99% in particulate matter compared with heavy fuel oil, depending on engine technology. Clarence Woo, managing director of the Global Centre for Green Fuels, said the US already had the production capacity and export infrastructure to supply ethanol to shipping at scale. (Source: Courtesy of Kjell-Bendik Pedersen) The European Union paid an estimated €8.7 billion for liquefied natural gas from Russia’s Yamal project in the first 10 months of 2026, exceeding the estimated total for all of 2025, as the countdown to a ban on Russian LNG imports enters its final weeks. EU ports received 12.89 million tonnes across 177 cargoes between January and October, up 6.3% from the same period last year, according to an analysis by environmental group Urgewald using Kpler shipping data. Europe accounted for 81% of Yamal’s recorded deliveries, underscoring the project’s continued dependence on the market it is about to lose. The estimated bill is around 21% higher than the €7.2 billion calculated for all of 2025 . The figures are indicative estimates based on monthly benchmark gas prices and delivered volumes, rather than verified contract payments. But the more immediate challenge for Yamal LNG, operated by Russian producer Novatek, is logistical. The EU ban on Russian LNG imports under eligible existing long-term contracts takes effect on January 1, forcing the project to redirect cargoes toward Asia just as winter ice makes eastbound navigation along the Northern Sea Route increasingly difficult. A Kpler analysis by principal commodity shipping analyst Igor Gavri? suggests there is still room for several additional European deliveries before the deadline. Based on vessel positions, historical movements, port restrictions and assumed sailing speeds, a tanker loading at Sabetta could theoretically complete around three additional deliveries to Zeebrugge before January 1. With transshipment to a conventional LNG carrier near Murmansk an Arc7 vessel could complete 4-5 additional deliveries. Russia has assembled a growing fleet of aging LNG vessels ahead of the ban. Kpler’s accompanying rotation model assumes 17 knots and four days in port per cycle. The analysis identifies plant output, rather than tanker availability, as the principal constraint on additional shipments. The deadline will produce a sharp change in a shipping system built around relatively short European voyages. Yamal depends on 14 specialized Arc7 ice-class LNG carriers, which can operate in Arctic waters and return quickly from nearby European terminals. During winter, conventional LNG carriers cannot reach Sabetta, while direct eastbound voyages to Asia become considerably more demanding. Since 2018, only 11 Arc7 cargoes have traveled east through the Northern Sea Route between November and May, Urgewald said. Russia is preparing to change that pattern. Rosatom expects regular year-round eastbound shipping along the Northern Sea Route to begin in early 2027 , coinciding with the arrival of an additional nuclear icebreaker and efforts by major exporters to establish regular deliveries to Asian markets. The nuclear-powered icebreaker Chukotka , the fourth serial Project 22220 vessel, is scheduled to enter service early next year, bringing Russia’s operational nuclear icebreaker fleet to nine. One likely operating model for Novatek and state-owned Atomflot is to use nuclear icebreakers to escort convoys of multiple Arc7 LNG carriers, improving the efficiency of scarce icebreaking capacity. After the European ban, Murmansk ship-to-ship transshipment and conventional LNG carriers are also expected to play a larger role , allowing Arc7 vessels to return to Sabetta rather than undertaking longer voyages to Asian customers. The transition to year-round eastbound NSR deliveries is far from guaranteed. Russia previously targeted year-round eastbound navigation for 2024 but failed to establish regular service. March and April remain particularly difficult, and a single additional icebreaker alone will not resolve constraints involving convoy speeds and icebreaker redundancy. October deliveries to Europe totaled 705,591 tonnes across 10 cargoes, worth an estimated €839 million. France received seven shipments, while Spain and the Netherlands received two and one, respectively. The January ban will not necessarily stop Yamal LNG exports, but it will remove the project’s most convenient winter market. European firms will be permitted to continue transporting and selling Yamal products outside of the EU. An earlier proposed complete ban on providing services to the Russian LNG sector was subsequently weakened by the EU. The completion of the corporate restructuring, which was first announced on May 26, 2026, follows receipt of the required South African regulatory approvals and joint venture partner consents, enabling Impact to become a pure-play Namibia-focused explorer and marking a further step in Meren’s strategy to simplify its business and high-grade its portfolio around its core areas of value creation in the Orange Basin. articles.body: Americas Dry Cargo Brazilian soybean exports smash records Sam Chambers November 12, 2026 0 601 1 minute read Norden Norden Brazilian soybean exports have smashed all previous records, with shipments during the first ten months of 2026 already exceeding the whole of last year’s total, providing a significant boost to dry bulk shipping demand, primarily panamaxes and supramaxes. Brazilian government customs data independently confirms the record-breaking trend, although its figures differ slightly from Ursa’s vessel-tracking estimates. Official exports reached 106.5m tonnes through October, up 5.9% year-on-year, generating $46bn in export revenue. The outlook suggests further records could follow. The US Department of Agriculture’s latest forecasts put Brazil’s 2026/27 soybean harvest at 186m tonnes, with exports projected to reach 118m tonnes. The growth is being driven primarily by increased acreage rather than higher yields, with harvested area forecast to expand to 50m hectares. Brazil’s own crop agency, Conab, is more conservative, projecting production of approximately 181.6m tonnes. With China remaining the dominant destination for Brazilian soybeans, further export growth has the potential to support tonne-mile demand well into 2027, something that will be under the microscope when the Agri-Commodities panel reconvenes on April 28 at Geneva Dry , the world’s premier commodities shipping conference. articles.body: Contributions Finance and Insurance Why shipowners might be better off sharing profits than taking on debt Splash November 12, 2026 0 448 3 minutes read Traditional loans demand repayments regardless of freight markets. Earnings-sharing structures offer a different proposition: investors participate in a vessel’s fortunes while owners retain control. Captain Vikas Pandey from Shipfinex explains. Ship finance looks healthy on paper. Petrofin Research estimates that the top 40 shipping banks grew their portfolios by 6% in 2025 to $300.6bn, and puts total ship finance across banks, leasing, export credit and alternative lenders at around $680bn. Societe Generale expects 2026 to remain a borrower’s market, with top-tier owners seeing margins of 100 to 150 basis points over SOFR. That is accurate for owners at the top. It is less accurate for the rest. Petrofin’s index of global bank ship finance stands at 63 against 100 in 2008, while the value of the fleet and orderbook has risen to about $2.17trn. Small and mid-sized owners, who by one industry estimate own up to 60% of the world’s ships, still meet low advance ratios on older tonnage, higher margins, or alternative lenders asking for equity kickers and profit participation on top of interest. For these owners, a third structure is worth understanding: selling a share of a single vessel’s future net earnings to outside investors, while the owner keeps title, management and commercial control. Cost. Where an owner can borrow at today’s bank margins, debt is almost always cheaper. Investors taking freight-market risk expect returns closer to equity. The comparison changes when the realistic alternative is private credit priced well above bank debt, with fees, tighter covenants and a profit share attached. At that point the owner is already paying for equity risk while still carrying the rigidity of a loan. Cash flow. This is the bigger difference. Debt service is fixed. Amortisation often runs shorter than the vessel’s remaining economic life, a balloon creates refinancing risk at maturity, and a minimum value clause can force prepayment or extra security when asset values fall. None of this adjusts when the charter market softens. An earnings share does. Investors receive an agreed percentage of net operating cash flow, so distributions fall when rates fall, and a weak quarter is not a default event. For an owner whose main exposure is a liquidity squeeze in a downturn, rather than the headline cost of capital, that flexibility has real value. Control. Investors in an earnings-share structure hold an economic right, not title. The vessel typically sits in a single-ship SPV that remains the registered owner, and the owner keeps technical and commercial management, crewing and chartering. Investors receive regular reporting and a vote on a short list of reserved matters, such as a sale of the vessel, new borrowing or a change of manager. A lender’s covenants, by contrast, can restrict distributions, require consent for employment and accelerate the loan on breach. Both structures constrain the owner, in different places. When it fits. Earnings-sharing tends to make sense where bank debt is unavailable or priced close to equity; where the vessel has visible employment, such as a period charter, that investors can underwrite; where the owner needs to protect liquidity through the cycle; or where equity is locked in an unencumbered vessel that the owner wants to release without selling. For an owner with cheap bank finance and a firm view that rates will rise, it gives away upside. Before signing, owners should settle the definition of net earnings and deductible costs, the treatment of off-hire and drydocking, reserve funding, the term and any cap on investor returns, buy-back rights, and what happens on a sale or total loss. Where a first-priority registered ship mortgage is in place, the mortgagee’s consent is required and investor distributions rank behind debt service. Debt remains the cheapest capital in shipping for owners who can get it on good terms. For many who cannot, sharing earnings matches the cost of capital to the way a ship actually earns its money. articles.body: Containers Europe Maersk hit by fresh cyber breach Adis Ajdin November 12, 2026 0 2,919 1 minute read Cydome Cydome Danish shipping giant AP Moller-Maersk has confirmed another cybersecurity breach after hackers gained access to an older IT system and extracted data, nearly a decade after the devastating NotPetya attack that cost the company up to $300m. The Copenhagen-headquartered group said on Wednesday that the incident involved a local legacy system inherited through a previous acquisition. Maersk’s cybersecurity team launched an investigation after discovering the intrusion and has taken steps to secure the affected system.”Our findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed,” the company said. The carrier said the breach appeared to be confined to the legacy system, with no indication that other Maersk systems or those belonging to customers and partners connected through APIs and electronic data interchange (EDI) had been compromised. The company added that it does not expect disruption to customer operations, with its digital booking and shipment management platforms continuing to operate normally. Maersk has not identified the acquired business involved, disclosed what data was extracted or named those responsible for the intrusion. The announcement follows separate claims by a hacker group calling itself WhiteArmor that it had obtained around 100 GB of logistics data from a platform associated with LF Logistics, the Hong Kong-based logistics business Maersk acquired for $3.6bn in 2022. The group has reportedly demanded $5m in bitcoin. The claims remain unverified, and Maersk has not confirmed any connection between the alleged theft and the incident it is investigating. The latest breach brings back memories of June 2017, when the NotPetya malware attack crippled Maersk’s IT infrastructure and disrupted container shipping and terminal operations worldwide. The Danish group subsequently put the financial damage at between $250m and $300m, making it one of the costliest cyber incidents in shipping history.
